questions.text: The first minutes: BLS, airway and breathing

steps.bridge: That was the bystander's sequence. Now you arrive, and you are trained. What changes?

lesson.text:
The heart has stopped. From this second there is one source of blood flow in the whole body, and it is somebody's hands on the chest. Everything in this first section is about getting those hands there quickly, and then not letting anything take them off.

Start outside the hospital, with a bystander and an adult who has just collapsed. The order is short. First, is the scene safe? A rescuer who is electrocuted or hit by traffic is a second patient. Second, check for a response: tap the shoulders and shout. Third, if there is none, shout for help, call the emergency number with the phone on speaker, and send someone for an AED. Fourth, look at the breathing. Fifth, if it isn't normal, start compressions.

Now the reasons. Why the speaker? Because the dispatcher can coach compressions while they are being given, and the guidelines of twenty twenty-five tell a lone rescuer with a mobile to call and start at once. Why send for the AED so early? Because an adult who collapses suddenly is most likely in ventricular fibrillation. What that needs is a shock, and the chance of survival falls with every minute it waits.

And why no pulse check for the bystander? Because even trained staff are poor at it. They miss weak pulses and imagine absent ones. So the lay rescuer gets a simpler rule.

[[Unresponsive and not breathing normally is cardiac arrest. A lay rescuer starts compressions on that alone, with no pulse check. A trained provider may check, but for no more than ten seconds.]]

The words 'not normally' carry the weight. In the first minutes of an arrest the brainstem still fires slow, noisy, irregular gasps. Your card says they occur in up to forty per cent of witnessed arrests; the newest guideline quotes forty to sixty. Either way they are the commonest reason a bystander waits. A gasp is not a breath. It is a sign of arrest.

That is the adult rule: call first, because the problem is electrical. The exam tests the exception. A five-year-old is pulled from a pool, unresponsive and not breathing. This heart didn't fibrillate. It ran out of oxygen. So the answer is CPR with a focus on rescue breathing, and the European guideline begins with five rescue breaths before settling into thirty compressions to two breaths. Ninety-one per cent got that one.

[[A sudden collapse in an adult is call first and fetch the AED. Drowning, asphyxia and most arrests in children are care first: breaths early, because oxygen is what is missing, not a shock.]]

NEET's favourite wrong option here is abdominal thrusts to drain water from the lungs. Very little water is aspirated, and thrusts only delay ventilation and bring up the stomach contents. The other wrong option is high-flow oxygen by mask while you watch for breathing. A mask moves no air into a child who isn't breathing.

One refinement. A lone rescuer with no phone, facing a hypoxic arrest, gives about two minutes of CPR before leaving to call. With a phone, it is speaker on and start.

steps.bridge: Compressions have started. Whether the coming shock works now depends on how often the hands come off.

lesson.text:
For you, the trained provider, two things change and one does not.

The first change is what activating the system means. In hospital it is the code team. Outside, in India, the ambulance number is one zero eight and the single emergency number is one one two. The source of your card printed one zero nine, which is neither.

The second change is that you do feel for a pulse. The carotid, at the same time as you watch the chest for breathing, for no more than ten seconds. And there is a rule for doubt: no definite pulse means start CPR. Why so strict? Because feeling longer doesn't make the answer more reliable, and the two mistakes are not equal. Compressing a patient who has a pulse costs little. Thirty seconds without flow in a patient who has none costs a great deal.

What does not change is the gasp. Unresponsive, with occasional gasps and no definite pulse in ten seconds, in an ICU bed or on a pavement, is an arrest. The answer is to start compressions.

Now the order, which Marrow asks directly. The sequence is C, A, B: compressions, then airway, then breathing. Thirty compressions come before the airway is opened and before any breath. The reason is the one from the last card. In a sudden cardiac arrest the blood sitting in the arteries is still full of oxygen. What is missing is flow. Opening the airway and giving two breaths first only delays the one thing that helps.

[[Adult BLS runs C, A, B. Compressions start first, thirty of them, because in a sudden arrest the blood is still oxygenated and the problem is flow. Breaths come after.]]

Two wrong options are built on this. 'Begin rescue breaths first' is the old A, B, C order, which was abandoned in twenty ten. And 'check the rhythm first' sounds like advanced practice, but the monitor is attached when it arrives. Compressions start now, before anyone knows the rhythm.

steps.bridge: That was a patient with no pulse. Next, the collapse where the pulse is still there, and what the AED tells you.

lesson.text:
Why do pauses matter so much? Here is the mechanism, and it runs through this whole packet.

Heart muscle is fed through the coronary arteries, and during CPR they fill only in the release phase, between compressions. The pressure that drives that filling is built slowly. Each compression adds a little to the pressure in the aorta, and it takes many in a row to reach a useful level. Stop, and that pressure collapses within seconds. Start again, and you begin from the bottom.

So a pause is not just lost seconds. It is lost pressure, and the compressions after it are spent rebuilding what you had.

[[Coronary perfusion pressure falls within seconds of stopping compressions and takes many compressions to rebuild. Every pause, before or after a shock, lowers the chance that the shock works.]]

Four targets follow from that.

The pre-shock pause, from the last compression to the shock, should be as short as possible. The American guideline leaves it there. The European one puts a number on it: under five seconds. You achieve it by charging the defibrillator while compressions continue, so the hands come off only for the word 'clear' and the shock itself.

The post-shock pause should be as short as possible too. Compressions resume immediately, with no rhythm check and no pulse check. A heart that has just been shocked is stunned. Even when the rhythm is now organised, it rarely pumps well for the first minute. It needs perfusion, not inspection.

The chest compression fraction is the share of the whole resuscitation during which someone is actually compressing. The target is at least sixty per cent. Good teams pass eighty, but sixty is the guideline minimum, and sixty is the number to know.

And rhythm checks come every two minutes, timed with the change of compressor, because depth begins to fall at about two minutes as the compressor tires. One pause does two jobs.

The evidence is worth one sentence. In twenty eleven Cheskes studied eight hundred and fifteen shockable arrests outside hospital. A pre-shock pause of twenty seconds or more, against under ten, roughly halved the odds of surviving to discharge, and each extra five seconds cost about eighteen per cent.

Now the bank question, which only thirty-six per cent got right. Which statement about defibrillation is false? Three of the options are true, and each sounds doubtful. A shock works best when fibrillation has lasted only a minute or two, before the muscle is depleted: true. Repeated shocks lower the impedance of the chest only slightly, by about eight per cent or less: true, and one reason stacked shocks add little. The false one is that the perishock pause is directly proportional to survival.

[[The perishock pause is the pre-shock pause plus the post-shock pause. It is inversely related to survival: the longer the hands are off around a shock, the fewer survive.]]

steps.bridge: Some patients can't breathe because something is in the way. That is the next collapse to sort.

lesson.text:
Now put the sequence together the way the exam writes it: a trained provider, an adult down in a hospital corridor.

Scene safe, check for a response. Then shout for help, activate the emergency system and send for the AED. Then check breathing and pulse together, for up to ten seconds.

The order of those last two is tested, and only sixty-three per cent got it right on a mini test. Help and the AED come before the pulse check. Why? Because once a lone rescuer has started CPR, they can't go and fetch a defibrillator without stopping. So the call goes out first.

The ten-second check has three possible results.

A pulse and normal breathing: watch the patient.

No definite pulse: CPR at thirty to two, and the AED goes on the moment it arrives.

And the third, the one NEET likes. A definite carotid pulse, but no breathing, or only gasps. This is respiratory arrest, not cardiac arrest. The heart is still making its own flow. What is missing is oxygen. So there are no compressions. You give rescue breaths, one every six seconds, which is ten a minute, and you recheck the pulse every two minutes. If the pulse goes, you start CPR. And you think of an opioid, and of naloxone.

[[A definite pulse with absent or gasping breathing is respiratory arrest: one breath every six seconds and a pulse check every two minutes. No definite pulse in ten seconds is CPR at thirty to two.]]

The wrong option is 'begin thirty to two' in a patient with a definite pulse. It was offered in two of your Grand Tests. Notice also how slow the rate is. Ten breaths a minute, not twenty. Every breath you push in raises the pressure in the chest and holds back venous return, so you give only as many as the oxygen needs.

Then the AED arrives and analyses. If it advises a shock, you shock and go straight back to compressions. If it says 'no shock advised', you also go straight back to compressions, for two minutes, with no pulse check.

Read that message correctly. 'No shock advised' doesn't mean the patient has a pulse. It means the rhythm isn't ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia. It is asystole or pulseless electrical activity, and both of those need compressions.

[[After any AED analysis or shock, resume CPR at once for two minutes. Don't check the pulse and don't repeat the shock first.]]

The same rule covers the stem where the AED has just delivered one shock for VF. The wrong options are 'check the pulse' and 'shock again'. The answer is two minutes of CPR.

steps.bridge: That sequence was for adults. Three bodies change the second manoeuvre: the child, the infant and the pregnant woman.

lesson.text:
In choking the heart is fine and the airway is blocked. The whole algorithm turns on one question: is air still moving?

A patient who can cough forcefully and speak is still moving air. Leave them alone, encourage the cough and watch. A forceful cough clears an airway better than anything you can do from outside, and a slap or a thrust at that stage can turn a partial obstruction into a complete one.

Severe obstruction has five signs. A weak or absent cough. Unable to speak. A change in colour, meaning cyanosis. Altered mental status. And apnoea. When any of these appears, the first action is to activate the emergency response, because your manoeuvres may fail and within minutes this patient may need CPR, suction and airway equipment.

Then, in the responsive adult, the sequence of twenty twenty-five: five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts, in repeated cycles, until the object comes out or the patient becomes unresponsive.

Here is the old answer and the new one. For years the American teaching for an adult was abdominal thrusts alone, the Heimlich manoeuvre, while the European teaching began with back blows. In twenty twenty-five the American guideline moved to back blows first, because in the evidence they relieved the obstruction more often and caused fewer injuries. An abdominal thrust can tear the liver, the spleen or the stomach. That is also why a patient is still observed after the object has come out.

[[Severe choking in a responsive adult, twenty twenty-five: call for help, then cycles of five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts. 'Abdominal thrusts first' is the older answer.]]

Now the moment the exam tests. The patient goes limp. Everything changes. You lower them to the ground and start CPR, beginning with compressions. Not more back blows, and not more thrusts. Why compressions? Because a chest compression generates an airway pressure at least as high as an abdominal thrust, so it works as a clearing manoeuvre and as circulation at once.

Before each set of breaths, look in the mouth. Take out what you can see. Never sweep blindly with a finger, because that can push the object deeper.

[[The moment a choking patient becomes unresponsive, it is CPR starting with compressions. Look in the mouth before the breaths and remove only an object you can see.]]

Marrow asked exactly this. A three-year-old choking on a peanut becomes unresponsive. The next step is chest compressions.

steps.bridge: The airway is clear of objects. Now, in the arrested patient, how do you hold it open and get air in?

lesson.text:
The first manoeuvre is now the same in everyone: five back blows. Only the second one changes, and it changes for an anatomical reason each time.

In adults and children, the second manoeuvre is five abdominal thrusts. The abdomen can be encircled, and the thrust pushes the diaphragm up and raises the pressure in the chest. Before twenty twenty-five, children in the American scheme got abdominal thrusts alone. Now they get back blows first, like adults.

In infants, the second manoeuvre is five chest thrusts, given with the heel of one hand. Abdominal thrusts are not used, because an infant's liver and spleen sit low, under a soft rib cage that doesn't protect them. That part isn't new. What is new in twenty twenty-five is the hand. The old two-finger technique has gone, for chest thrusts and for infant compressions alike, because two fingers did not reach an adequate depth.

In late pregnancy, or in anyone whose abdomen you can't get your arms around, the second manoeuvre is again five chest thrusts, over the lower sternum. A thrust into a pregnant abdomen lands on the uterus.

{{**Who | After 5 back blows**
Adult, child | 5 abdominal thrusts
Infant | 5 chest thrusts, heel of one hand
Late pregnancy, large abdomen | 5 chest thrusts
Anyone unresponsive | CPR, compressions first}}

[[Back blows first for everyone. Then abdominal thrusts for adults and children, and chest thrusts for infants, for late pregnancy and for an abdomen that cannot be encircled.]]

The Grand Test stem was a woman in her third trimester, conscious, unable to speak, with a weak cough. The answer is cycles of five back blows followed by five chest thrusts. One wrong option gives her abdominal thrusts. The other starts CPR immediately, and CPR is for the unresponsive patient. While she is conscious, it is blows and thrusts.

steps.bridge: The airway is open. The next question is how much to breathe for the patient, and the answer is less than you think.

lesson.text:
Compressions give you flow. That flow is only worth having if the blood passing through the lungs picks up oxygen. So now the airway, and the principle is simple: use the simplest thing that works, because every more complex device costs compression time.

Start with why an unconscious airway closes. The tongue and the epiglottis fall back against the pharynx. Lifting the jaw pulls the tongue forward. So the basic manoeuvre is head tilt and chin lift, and the two adjuncts hold that position for you. An oropharyngeal airway is for the patient with no gag reflex, because otherwise it provokes vomiting. A nasopharyngeal airway is tolerated by a patient who is half awake, but you avoid it in a suspected fracture of the skull base or a severe coagulopathy.

Now the ladder, from simple to complex. Compression-only CPR. Mouth to mouth. Bag and mask. Those three are basic. Then the line, and beyond it the advanced airways: a supraglottic airway, and then a tracheal tube. The border between basic and advanced sits just after the bag and mask.

The bag and mask is the step most often done badly, and a Grand Test asked for its main limitation. It is gastric inflation. When the pressure in the pharynx rises above about twenty centimetres of water, the lower oesophageal sphincter opens and the air goes into the stomach. The stomach fills, the diaphragm is splinted, and regurgitation follows. So each breath is given slowly, over one second, with just enough volume to see the chest rise. The wrong options are tracheal injury, and that it needs two rescuers. Two rescuers make it better. They are not required.

[[The main limitation of bag-mask ventilation is gastric inflation, once pharyngeal pressure passes about twenty centimetres of water. Give each breath over one second, with only visible chest rise.]]

Beyond the line, which device? In arrest the outcomes with a supraglottic airway and with a tube are similar. So the choice depends on the system. Where intubation success is low, or practice is infrequent, the supraglottic airway is preferred, because it goes in faster with fewer pauses in compressions. The tube is for systems with high success rates. NEET's wrong option is that intubation is always the preferred advanced airway.

One point of vocabulary, because your card mixes two words. Advanced life support calls any supraglottic airway or tube an advanced airway. A definitive airway, in trauma teaching, is strictly a cuffed tube below the cords. A supraglottic device sits above them and doesn't fully protect against aspiration.

Last, the neck. In suspected injury to the cervical spine, you open the airway with a jaw thrust, without tilting the head, because it moves the neck least. But the rule of twenty twenty-five is plain. If a jaw thrust and an adjunct don't open the airway, a trained rescuer should use head tilt and chin lift. A closed airway kills in minutes. A cord injury made worse by some extension is uncommon.

[[In head and neck trauma the jaw thrust comes first. If it fails even with an adjunct, use head tilt and chin lift: an airway that stays closed is the more urgent threat.]]

The NEET recall asked the whole trauma sequence in order. Suction first. Then jaw thrust or chin lift. Then an oral or nasal airway. Then a cuffed tube with manual in-line stabilisation, and a surgical airway if intubation fails. Any option that puts the advanced airway before suction and the basic manoeuvres is wrong. And when the recall listed chin lift, a Guedel airway and a supraglottic device and asked which is not used to maintain an airway, the answer was none. All of them are.

steps.bridge: Flow and oxygen are running. Section two asks what the monitor shows, and whether electricity can end it.

lesson.text:
In an arrest the danger with ventilation isn't too little. It is too much.

Here is why. Blood returns to the chest because the pressure inside it is low. Every breath you push in raises that pressure and holds venous return back. During CPR the output is already a fraction of normal, so a big breath, or too many, takes away the filling your compressions depend on. Less filling means less flow to the coronaries and to the brain. Over-ventilation also washes out carbon dioxide, and a low carbon dioxide constricts the brain's vessels.

That is the answer to a question only thirty-one per cent got right. During CPR with a bag and mask, which action best protects cerebral perfusion? Avoiding hyperinflation with each breath. Each breath is given over one second, about five to six hundred millilitres, just enough to see the chest rise. The tempting wrong option was 'deliver ten breaths a minute'. That number is real, but it belongs to a different situation.

[[With a bag and mask the ratio is thirty compressions to two breaths. One breath every six seconds, ten a minute, applies only once an advanced airway is in, with compressions then continuous.]]

Now oxygen. During CPR you give all you can, a hundred per cent, and there is no saturation target at all. The pulse oximeter is unreliable without a pulse, and when flow is this low the only lever left on oxygen delivery is how much each millilitre of blood carries. Hyperoxia only becomes a concern when flow returns. After ROSC you titrate to a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight per cent. The older figure, from twenty twenty, was ninety-two to ninety-eight, and the European guideline uses ninety-four to ninety-eight. During the arrest itself, any option that titrates oxygen to a target is wrong.

Next, the tube. How do you know it is in the trachea? By waveform capnography. A sustained waveform over several breaths means carbon dioxide is coming from the lungs. A tube in the oesophagus gives a few shrinking waves and then nothing. Seeing the tube pass the cords, watching the chest move and listening to breath sounds can all mislead.

The chest X-ray answers a different question. It shows depth, with the tip two to five centimetres above the carina. It can't exclude a tube in the oesophagus.

[[Waveform capnography confirms that the tube is in the trachea. The chest X-ray confirms only its depth. If capnography is among the options, choose it.]]

Be careful with one NEET recall. The stem said the cords had been seen, a colour-change carbon dioxide detector was positive and breath sounds were equal, and it asked for the best verification of proper position. The keyed answer was the chest radiograph, because carbon dioxide had already been shown and only depth was left to check.

Finally the capnograph's second job. During CPR the end-tidal carbon dioxide should be at least ten millimetres of mercury, and ideally twenty or more. What that number is really measuring comes in the next section.

spine: Unresponsive + not breathing normally (gasps count) = arrest. Adult: call, AED, compress; drowning/child: breaths early (ERC 5 rescue breaths). C-A-B.
Pulse check ≤10 s. Help and AED before the check. Pulse but no breathing → 1 breath/6 s. After any shock or 'no shock advised' → CPR 2 min, no pulse check.
Pauses kill coronary perfusion pressure: pre-shock as short as possible (ERC <5 s), CCF ≥60%, rhythm check every 2 min; perishock pause is INVERSELY related to survival.
Choking 2025: 5 back blows → 5 abdominal thrusts; infant, late pregnancy, large abdomen → chest thrusts; unresponsive → CPR, look before breaths, no blind sweep.
Airway ladder: tilt/jaw thrust → OPA/NPA → bag-mask (limit: gastric inflation) | SGA → ETT. Low intubation success → SGA. Trauma: jaw thrust, then head tilt if it fails.
Breathing: 100% O₂, no SpO₂ target in arrest; 30:2 with a bag, 10/min only with an advanced airway; avoid hyperinflation. Capnography = trachea; X-ray = depth.

open.text:
This is the last packet, and it starts where every other packet could have ended. A man collapses in a corridor. No pulse. No breathing, or only a gasp.

In Shock One you learned that every shock is one of three numbers failing: filling, pump or squeeze. Cardiac arrest is what happens when all three fail at once. The pump has stopped, so there's no flow. The vessels lose their tone. And without flow there's no filling either. Everything you do in an arrest is a way of giving those three numbers back, by hand and by drug, until the heart can take them over again.

[[In an arrest, your hands are the pump, adrenaline restores the squeeze, and finding the reversible cause gives back the filling.]]

This packet is long, because arrest is where NEET sets a great many questions, and because the guidelines changed in twenty twenty-five. Old numbers and new ones both still circulate in the question banks. So whenever a number changed, you'll hear the twenty twenty-five answer first, and the older one named as the trap.

It runs in the order an arrest happens. The first minutes: basic life support, the airway and breathing. Then the rhythms and the shocks. Then the drugs, vascular access, the reversible causes, and when to stop. Then the special arrests: pregnancy, asthma, heat and cold, and when to put him on ECMO. Then the hours after the heart restarts. Then temperature control and shivering. And last, the question every family asks: will he wake up?

Two grand-test misses sit in this packet, one in the section on drugs and access, and one in the hours after ROSC. Listen for them.

Start in the corridor. What do you do in the first ten seconds?

steps.bridge: Ventricular tachycardia comes in two shapes, and the shape decides how you shock it. First, the uniform one.

lesson.text:
Four rhythms. Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shocked. Pulseless electrical activity, PEA, and asystole are not. To see why, ask what a shock really does.

A shock doesn't start a heart. It stops one. A defibrillating shock depolarises almost all the myocardium in the same instant. That wipes out whatever chaotic or circling activity was there, and in the silence that follows, the sinus node has a chance to take charge again. So a shock can only help when there is disorganised or re-entrant electrical activity to erase.

Ventricular fibrillation is exactly that. The ventricles quiver, with no coordinated contraction. It may be coarse, with large waves, or fine, with small ones as the muscle runs out of energy. Either way it produces no output at all. The bank has asked it twice: which rhythm can never support perfusion? Ventricular fibrillation.

The wrong option beside it is ventricular tachycardia. VT often does carry a pulse. With a pulse it is treated by synchronised cardioversion or by drugs, as you learned in the rhythm packet. It becomes a shockable arrest rhythm only when the pulse is gone.

[[Ventricular fibrillation never perfuses. Ventricular tachycardia may, so it is defibrillated only when pulseless. With a pulse it is cardioverted or treated with drugs.]]

Now the two that are not shocked. In asystole there is no electrical activity, so there is nothing to erase. In PEA the electrical activity is organised, and a shock can't improve on organised. The fault lies elsewhere: an empty heart, an obstructed heart, or muscle too poisoned to contract. Shocking either rhythm achieves one thing, a pause in compressions.

Last, the third part of your card. Where do atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter and supraventricular tachycardia belong? Not on this list. They are rhythms that perfuse, and in an unstable patient with a pulse they are cardioverted. So what if the monitor shows atrial fibrillation and there is no pulse? Then you are looking at organised electrical activity without a pulse. By definition that is PEA. It gets CPR and adrenaline, not a shock.

[[Any organised rhythm without a pulse is PEA, atrial fibrillation included. Defibrillation is unsynchronised and for the pulseless. Cardioversion is synchronised and for a patient who still has a pulse.]]

One more stem from the bank. A pregnant woman arrests, and you're shown strips and asked which needs immediate defibrillation. The answer is pulseless VT, and pregnancy changes nothing about that.

steps.bridge: That was one circuit and one shape. When the shape changes from beat to beat, the shock changes too.

lesson.text:
You read this rhythm in the rhythm packet, so this is a reminder, with the arrest in mind.

Monomorphic VT is a regular, broad-complex tachycardia in which every QRS in a lead looks the same. Each part of that has a cause. It is broad, usually over a hundred and twenty milliseconds, because the impulse starts in the ventricle and spreads slowly from muscle cell to muscle cell instead of down the fast conducting system. It is uniform because there is one focus or one circuit, so activation takes the same path every beat. Remember where that circuit usually lives: at the edge of an old infarct scar, which is where the second ACS packet left you.

The exceptions to the uniformity are the proof of the diagnosis. Now and then an atrial impulse slips through the AV node. If it captures the ventricles on its own, you see one normal narrow beat: a capture beat. If it meets the VT wavefront halfway, you see a hybrid: a fusion beat. Both show that the atria and ventricles are beating independently, and that proves VT.

[[A regular, broad-complex tachycardia with identical beats is monomorphic VT. Fusion and capture beats prove it. In a patient with ischaemic heart disease, broad and regular is VT until shown otherwise.]]

The Grand Test stem was a man with ischaemic heart disease and chest pain, a wide QRS, no P waves and a rate of a hundred and fifty. Eighty-eight per cent called it VT. The wrong options were atrial flutter and atrial fibrillation. Flutter and fibrillation are narrow unless there is aberrant conduction, and fibrillation is irregular.

For the arrest, one thing matters. A monomorphic VT has an R wave the machine can find. So with a pulse it can be cardioverted in synchrony. Without a pulse, it is defibrillated like VF.

steps.bridge: Those were the ventricular rhythms. One card on the atrial ones, so that you never shock them as arrest rhythms.

lesson.text:
In polymorphic VT the QRS changes from beat to beat in amplitude, axis and duration, because activation takes a different path every time. Your card puts it as multiple ventricular foci.

Start with what that does to the shock. A synchronised shock needs a consistent R wave to time itself on. Here there isn't one. The synchroniser may fail to fire at all, or fire on a T wave. So polymorphic VT is always shocked unsynchronised, at high energy. That is defibrillation, whether or not there is a pulse.

[[Polymorphic VT is never cardioverted in synchrony. Sustained polymorphic VT gets an immediate unsynchronised shock at maximum energy, because the machine cannot track a changing QRS.]]

The guideline of twenty twenty-five goes one step further and says all polymorphic VT is to be treated as unstable. So a Grand Test key that looked disputed, polymorphic VT with a pulse and the most critical action, is right: an unsynchronised shock.

Now the cause, because it decides the drug. Measure the QT interval on a sinus beat.

If the QT is normal, the commonest cause is ischaemia or infarction. You treat the ischaemia, and the drugs are amiodarone or lidocaine. Magnesium does nothing here.

If the QT is long, this is torsades de pointes, a twisting of the points: the complexes seem to turn around the baseline. A long QT means slow, uneven repolarisation. Early afterdepolarisations then trigger extra beats, typically after a pause, and more easily with a slow heart rate, low potassium or low magnesium. The usual triggers are drugs that block the potassium current: haloperidol, methadone, macrolides, sotalol, ondansetron.

The treatment is magnesium, two grams intravenously. It suppresses the afterdepolarisations without shortening the QT, and it can be repeated. Stop the offending drugs and correct the potassium. If torsades keeps returning after that, raise the heart rate, by overdrive pacing or isoproterenol, because a faster rate shortens the QT. And never give amiodarone or sotalol, which lengthen it.

{{**Polymorphic VT in a stem | Answer**
Pulseless, unstable or sustained | unsynchronised shock, maximum energy
Long QT, recurring, patient stable | magnesium 2 g IV, repeat; stop QT drugs; K⁺
Recurs despite magnesium | overdrive pacing or isoproterenol
Normal QT | treat ischaemia; amiodarone or lidocaine}}

The bank has four questions here. A stable ICU patient with polymorphic VT and a corrected QT of five hundred and forty milliseconds: first-line drug, magnesium. The NEET recall with a twisting strip in a critically ill patient: torsades, magnesium sulphate.

And the hard one, at sixty per cent. A patient on haloperidol and methadone has torsades. It converts with magnesium, then recurs, and the patient is awake and talking. NEET's favourite wrong option is to go straight to pacing or cardioversion. The answer is more magnesium, with the two drugs stopped. Pacing comes only when magnesium has failed.

[[Torsades is polymorphic VT on a long QT: magnesium two grams, repeated, with the QT drugs stopped and potassium corrected. Amiodarone belongs to polymorphic VT with a normal QT, never to torsades.]]

steps.bridge: You know which rhythms are shocked. Now the machine: how much energy, and what the number depends on.

lesson.text:
This card is here for one reason: so that the atrial rhythms never get mistaken for arrest rhythms.

Atrial fibrillation is disorganised atrial activation, with many small re-entry circuits wandering through the atria and no coordinated atrial contraction. There is no P wave, the baseline shows fine fibrillatory waves, and the AV node is hit by impulses at random. So the ventricular rhythm is irregularly irregular. Stretched, scarred atria sustain those circuits, which is why the bank's patient, asked twice, is elderly with hypertension and heart failure.

Atrial flutter is one large re-entrant circuit, typically circling the right atrium at about three hundred a minute. That gives the sawtooth waves in the inferior leads. The AV node can't conduct three hundred a minute, so it lets through every second or third impulse, and the ventricular rate is often a regular hundred and fifty.

NEET's wrong option is 'irregular tachycardia with absent P waves is atrial flutter'. Flutter has flutter waves and is usually regular. Irregularly irregular with no P waves is fibrillation.

Both are supraventricular tachycardias, they often coexist, and they are treated alike: rate control, anticoagulation by stroke risk, and synchronised cardioversion when the patient is unstable. You met all of that in the rhythm packet.

One number has changed, and older banks still carry the old value. For atrial fibrillation the first synchronised shock is now at least two hundred joules, and for flutter two hundred joules. The older answers were a hundred and twenty to two hundred for fibrillation and fifty to a hundred for flutter. The reasoning is that a first shock that fails means more sedation time and more shocks.

[[Atrial fibrillation and flutter perfuse, so with a pulse they are cardioverted in synchrony, now starting at two hundred joules. Without a pulse the rhythm is PEA and is not shocked at all.]]

steps.bridge: You have the rhythms and the machine. Now run the shockable side of the algorithm in order.

lesson.text:
A defibrillator delivers a measured dose of electrical energy to the heart, to force it back towards a normal rhythm. You already know how: by depolarising a critical mass of myocardium at once. And you know what it can't do. It can't start a heart that has no electrical activity. That is why asystole is never shocked.

Now the dose, and it depends on the waveform.

A monophasic machine sends current in one direction only. It is less efficient, so every shock is the full three hundred and sixty joules.

A biphasic machine reverses the current halfway through the pulse. That defibrillates at a lower energy and injures less muscle, so biphasic is preferred. But the machines differ from one maker to another, so there isn't one biphasic number. The rule is to use the manufacturer's recommended dose, typically a first shock of a hundred and twenty to two hundred joules. And if you don't know the recommendation, use the maximum the machine offers. The logic is simple. Too little energy leaves the heart fibrillating, and that costs far more than the small risk of a larger shock.

[[Biphasic: the manufacturer's dose, about a hundred and twenty to two hundred joules, and the maximum available if that dose is unknown. Monophasic: three hundred and sixty joules every time.]]

For the second and later shocks, the dose should be at least equivalent, and a higher dose may be considered. A first shock that failed suggests a chest with high impedance or a heart that is hard to defibrillate, so stepping up, where the machine allows it, is reasonable. And one shock at a time. Three stacked shocks in a row is the old practice, and you saw why at the start: repeated shocks barely lower the impedance, and each one adds a pause.

The bank asks this card through pregnancy. A woman in the third trimester is in ventricular fibrillation: which statement about defibrillation is true? Standard energy, with no modification. Eighty-one per cent got it. The impedance of the chest doesn't change meaningfully in pregnancy, and very little current reaches the fetus. The wrong options halve the dose or avoid the shock.

A second trap is 'only biphasic is acceptable'. Biphasic is preferred. But a monophasic machine at three hundred and sixty joules is still the correct treatment if it is the machine you have. Any defibrillator now beats a better one later.

steps.bridge: Between the shocks, how do you know your compressions are doing anything? The capnograph tells you.

lesson.text:
Now the shockable side of the arrest algorithm, from start to finish. It is a loop of two minutes, and each turn of the loop adds one thing.

The rhythm is VF or pulseless VT. First shock. Then, at once, two minutes of CPR, and during those two minutes someone gets intravenous or intraosseous access. Nothing else goes in yet.

Rhythm check. Still shockable? Second shock. Two minutes of CPR, and now adrenaline, one milligram, repeated every three to five minutes. This is also when you consider an advanced airway and capnography.

Rhythm check. Still shockable? Third shock. Two minutes of CPR, and now the antiarrhythmic, amiodarone or lidocaine, and the search for a reversible cause.

So the order is shock, shock with adrenaline, shock with the antiarrhythmic. Why does adrenaline wait until after the second shock? Because in this rhythm the treatment that works is the shock. Adrenaline raises the heart's oxygen demand and, given before any shock, only delays defibrillation. Its job comes when shocks have failed. Then its squeeze on the vessels raises the aortic diastolic pressure and the coronary flow, which makes the next shock more likely to work.

[[Shockable rhythm: shock first, and again every two minutes. Adrenaline joins after the second shock, and amiodarone or lidocaine after the third.]]

That is the American order, and it is the one to answer with. The European algorithm gives both adrenaline and amiodarone after the third shock, so know that the difference exists.

After every shock, compressions resume immediately, with no pulse check, for the reason you already have: the heart that has just been defibrillated is stunned. And if at any rhythm check the rhythm is no longer shockable, you cross to the other side of the algorithm. If it is organised, you check for a pulse. If there is none, it is PEA.

The bank tested the first step with a distraction. A man goes into VF shortly after contact with a high-voltage line. Eighty-one per cent chose immediate defibrillation. The wrong options were amiodarone first, magnesium, and pacing. VF from any cause is defibrillated at once. Antiarrhythmics are for VF that persists after shocks. Magnesium is for torsades. And pacing has no role in VF.

[[Ventricular fibrillation from any cause, electrocution included, is defibrillated immediately. No drug comes before the first shock.]]

steps.bridge: The capnograph is one window on flow. The pressure it stands in for is the last idea of this section.

lesson.text:
Why would a monitor of breathing tell you about compressions? Follow the carbon dioxide.

The tissues make it. Blood carries it to the lungs. Ventilation blows it off. During CPR the ventilation is fixed, at ten breaths a minute, and the tissues go on making carbon dioxide. So the only thing that can change how much arrives at the lungs is how much blood arrives at the lungs. The end-tidal carbon dioxide becomes a meter of pulmonary blood flow. And pulmonary blood flow, in an arrest, is your compressions.

[[During CPR, with ventilation held constant, end-tidal carbon dioxide reflects pulmonary blood flow, which means compression quality. A low or falling value means improve the compressions.]]

So read it this way. A low or flat trace, around five to ten millimetres of mercury, means too little flow. Fix the compressions. The standard is a depth of five to six centimetres, two to two point four inches, at a hundred to a hundred and twenty a minute, with full recoil and no leaning. Under five centimetres is too shallow. Over six adds injury and no benefit.

The bank asked it twice. An intubated patient in PEA with a persistent end-tidal of eight despite correct ventilation: reassess and improve CPR quality. And an end-tidal drifting down from eighteen to seven over a few minutes with no change in rhythm: the compressor is tiring. Rotate, and push harder.

Three wrong options sit beside those answers. Giving bicarbonate, which isn't routine. Raising the ventilation rate, which lowers the number further and harms flow. And stopping the resuscitation. A low value on its own is never a reason to stop, and that returns in the next section.

Now the other direction. When the heart restarts, output jumps, and the carbon dioxide that has been building up in the tissues is washed to the lungs all at once. The end-tidal rises suddenly and stays up. Your card gives the classic figure, forty millimetres of mercury or more, which was printed on the algorithm of twenty twenty. The text of twenty twenty-five no longer prints forty. It says an abrupt rise, of more than ten millimetres of mercury, may indicate ROSC, which can happen below forty. So if the option says abrupt and sustained, choose it. If only a number is offered, forty is the keyed one.

[[An abrupt, sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide suggests ROSC: classically to forty millimetres of mercury or more, and in the text of twenty twenty-five a sudden jump of more than ten.]]

One false signal to know. A bolus of sodium bicarbonate releases carbon dioxide and raises the end-tidal briefly. That is chemistry, not a heartbeat.

steps.bridge: Shocks reset the rhythm and compressions feed the heart. Section three adds the drugs, and the search for a cause.

lesson.text:
Here is the pressure the whole first half of this packet has been pointing at.

The heart muscle is perfused between compressions, in the release phase. At that moment the pressure pushing blood into the coronary arteries is the diastolic pressure in the aorta. The pressure resisting it is the pressure in the right atrium, where the coronary veins drain. The difference between the two is the coronary perfusion pressure.

That number has a history. In nineteen ninety Paradis measured both pressures in a hundred patients during CPR. Nobody whose coronary perfusion pressure stayed below fifteen millimetres of mercury got a pulse back. So fifteen to twenty is the floor usually quoted, and coronary perfusion pressure is the best predictor of ROSC.

The bank asked it twice, and only fifty-eight and fifty-three per cent got it. A pulseless patient is receiving high-quality CPR: which parameter correlates best with ROSC? Coronary perfusion pressure.

[[Coronary perfusion pressure is aortic diastolic pressure minus right atrial diastolic pressure, in the release phase. It is the best predictor of ROSC, which is rare below fifteen to twenty millimetres of mercury.]]

Two wrong options are worth understanding. The first is the systolic, or peak, arterial pressure during compressions. The peak shows how hard you pushed. But the coronaries don't fill during the push. A high peak can sit on top of a heart that isn't being fed. The second is a palpable femoral pulse. The femoral vein runs beside the artery, and a compression sends a pressure wave back down the great veins as well as forward down the arteries. A pulse felt there may be venous, and it says nothing about coronary flow.

You can't measure coronary perfusion pressure at the bedside. So you watch two stand-ins. End-tidal carbon dioxide, which reports flow through the lungs. And, if an arterial line is in, the arterial diastolic pressure.

Here the numbers have moved, so take them in order. The guideline of twenty twenty said that if the arterial diastolic pressure was under twenty millimetres of mercury, you should improve the CPR. That is the figure in older banks, and it follows from Paradis. The American guideline of twenty twenty-five says the adult data are too thin to set any target. The European guideline of the same year suggests aiming for a diastolic of thirty or more, with an end-tidal of twenty-five or more. For the end-tidal, the American text keeps at least ten, ideally twenty.

{{**During CPR | AHA 2025 | ERC 2025**
ETCO₂ | ≥10, ideally ≥20 mmHg | ≥25 mmHg
Arterial diastolic | no adult target (2020: improve if <20) | ≥30 mmHg
Predictor of ROSC | CPP = aortic diastolic − RA diastolic, needs ≥15–20}}

[[During compressions, watch the diastolic pressure, not the systolic peak, and never trust a femoral pulse. The older target was a diastolic above twenty; in twenty twenty-five America sets no number and Europe says thirty.]]

The rest of the card is the practical order of circulation. Attach the monitor and defibrillator first, because the shock decides the shockable rhythms. Get access without stopping compressions. Then give the drugs.

spine: Shockable: VF (never perfuses) and pulseless VT. Non-shockable: asystole and PEA. Any organised rhythm without a pulse, AF included, is PEA.
Monomorphic VT: regular, broad, identical; fusion/capture beats prove it. Polymorphic VT: always unsynchronised shock. Long QT = torsades → Mg 2 g, repeat; no amiodarone.
Energy: biphasic per manufacturer (120–200 J), maximum if unknown; monophasic 360 J; same in pregnancy. AF cardioversion now ≥200 J, flutter 200 J.
Shockable loop: shock → CPR 2 min + access → shock → adrenaline 1 mg → shock → amiodarone or lidocaine. No pulse check after a shock.
ETCO₂ in CPR = flow: low/falling → better compressions (5–6 cm, 100–120/min); abrupt sustained rise → ROSC (classically ≥40; 2025: jump >10).
CPP = aortic diastolic − RA diastolic; best predictor of ROSC (≥15–20). Not systolic peak, not a femoral pulse. Diastolic target: AHA 2025 none; ERC ≥30.

open.text:
The hands are on the chest, the airway is open and oxygen is going in. All of that buys time. None of it restarts anything. This section is about the monitor: which rhythm is on it, and whether electricity can end it.

There are only four arrest rhythms. Two are shocked and two are not. So the whole section hangs on one sorting question, asked again every two minutes: is this rhythm shockable? If it is, the shock is the treatment and everything else supports it. If it isn't, a shock only costs you compressions.

[[Every two minutes the arrest asks one question: shockable or not? Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shocked. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity never are.]]

Listen for three traps as we go. A rhythm you would cardiovert in a patient with a pulse is not a rhythm you defibrillate in an arrest. The capnograph during CPR measures flow, not breathing. And the pressure that predicts the return of a pulse is not the systolic one.

Begin with the four rhythms.

questions.text: Drugs, access, causes and when to stop

steps.bridge: Adrenaline feeds the heart so the next shock can work. If the shocks still fail, one more class of drug is added.

lesson.text:
Why adrenaline at all? Go back to the pressure you just learned. The heart in arrest is fed by the gap between aortic diastolic pressure and right atrial pressure. Adrenaline's alpha effect squeezes the arterial tree, so more of the pressure from each compression stays in the aorta. The aortic diastolic pressure rises, and with it the flow to the coronaries. That is the whole reason it is given. In an arrest it is used as a vasoconstrictor, not as a stimulant.

When you give it depends on the rhythm.

In asystole and PEA there is no shock to give, and the chance of ROSC falls with every minute before the first dose. So it goes in as soon as you have access. You don't wait for the second rhythm check, or for an advanced airway, or for a capnography reading. The Grand Test keyed it as 'as soon as feasible'.

In VF and pulseless VT, the treatment that works is the shock. So adrenaline waits until the first shocks have failed, which in the American algorithm means after the second.

[[Adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm: as soon as possible. In a shockable rhythm: after the first shocks have failed, which means after the second shock. One milligram, every three to five minutes.]]

Now the dose, and the arithmetic that only thirty-four per cent got right. The adult dose is one milligram, intravenous or intraosseous, every three to five minutes. The question is which ampoule that is.

A strength of one in ten thousand means one gram in ten thousand millilitres. That is nought point one of a milligram per millilitre. So one milligram is ten millilitres. A strength of one in a thousand is one gram in a thousand millilitres, which is one milligram per millilitre. So one milligram is one millilitre, and ten millilitres would be ten milligrams, a tenfold overdose.

{{**Strength | Per mL | Use**
1:10,000 | 0.1 mg/mL | arrest: **10 mL = 1 mg** IV/IO
1:1000 | 1 mg/mL | anaphylaxis: **0.5 mL = 0.5 mg** IM
India: 1 mL of 1:1000 diluted to 10 mL = 1:10,000}}

[[The arrest dose of adrenaline is ten millilitres of one in ten thousand. One in a thousand is the intramuscular strength for anaphylaxis, at half a millilitre.]]

In India you often make it yourself: one millilitre from the one in a thousand ampoule, diluted to ten. NEET's wrong options are 'ten millilitres of one in a thousand' and 'one millilitre of one in a thousand' as the intravenous arrest preparation. And giving more doesn't help. High-dose adrenaline has no benefit.

The bank asks the same drug in a pregnant woman, twice, and the first time only fifty-four per cent were right. The first-line vasopressor in maternal arrest is adrenaline, one milligram every three to five minutes. The wrong options are phenylephrine, noradrenaline and dopamine. Pregnancy changes the patient's position and the site of the cannula. It doesn't change the drugs.

For children the dose is nought point nought one of a milligram per kilogram. That is nought point one of a millilitre per kilogram of the one in ten thousand solution, to a maximum of one milligram, at the same interval.

Last, vasopressin, which both the Grand Test and Marrow have asked. It once sat in the algorithm, at forty units, as a substitute for a dose of adrenaline. The idea was attractive, because it squeezes vessels through a different receptor that still works in acid blood. But the trials showed no better survival, alone or in combination. So the position now is that vasopressin offers no advantage as a substitute for adrenaline, and it is out of the algorithm. Any option that calls it first line, or better after a long arrest, is wrong.

steps.bridge: Those are the arrest drugs. One drug that people expect in the arrest algorithm is no longer there. Where did atropine go?

lesson.text:
Three shocks and adrenaline, and the monitor still shows VF. This is refractory VF, and now you add an antiarrhythmic. There are two choices, and the first thing to know is that they are alternatives.

Amiodarone is a class three drug. Its main action is to block potassium channels, which lengthens repolarisation and the refractory period. It also blocks sodium channels, calcium channels and beta receptors. The adult dose is a bolus of three hundred milligrams, and a second dose of a hundred and fifty.

Lidocaine is a class one B drug. It blocks fast sodium channels, binding and releasing quickly, so it acts mainly on ischaemic, partly depolarised muscle. That suits VF arising from an infarct. The adult dose is one to one point five milligrams per kilogram, then nought point five to nought point seven five, up to a maximum of three milligrams per kilogram.

[[Refractory VF or pulseless VT: amiodarone three hundred milligrams, then a hundred and fifty; or lidocaine one to one point five milligrams per kilogram, then half that. They are alternatives with the same outcome.]]

How do we know they are equal? From the ALPS trial of twenty sixteen, in shock-refractory arrest outside hospital. Survival to discharge was about twenty-four per cent with amiodarone, twenty-four with lidocaine and twenty-one with placebo, and the differences were not significant. More patients reached hospital alive with either drug. And in the arrests witnessed by a bystander, both drugs did better than placebo, which suggests they help when they are given early. So the recommendation is weak, and the wording is 'amiodarone or lidocaine'. The Grand Test asked for the preferred strategy after three shocks and two doses of adrenaline, and the key was exactly that: either one, with equivalent survival to discharge.

In children the doses are by weight: amiodarone five milligrams per kilogram, which can be given up to three times, and lidocaine one milligram per kilogram.

Now a keyed answer you should know is imperfect. A woman at thirty weeks with eclampsia and status epilepticus goes into VF. Which pair of drugs? The key is amiodarone with magnesium, and sixty-seven per cent chose it. The option marked wrong was lidocaine with magnesium, and by the guideline it is just as correct. The fear behind the key is that amiodarone affects the fetal thyroid, but that doesn't matter in an arrest. So with both pairs on offer, pick the amiodarone pair. And keep the principle: pregnancy doesn't change the arrest drugs.

One more wrong option is a procainamide infusion. Procainamide belongs to stable VT with a pulse. In an arrest its benefit is uncertain.

[[With no amiodarone available in refractory VF, the alternative is lidocaine, not procainamide. Procainamide is for stable VT with a pulse.]]

steps.bridge: You know the drugs and the doses. Now the route: which line, and what to do when the veins fail.

lesson.text:
Atropine was in the asystole algorithm for decades. The idea was that excessive vagal tone might be holding the heart still. The trials found no benefit, because in asystole vagal tone isn't the problem, and in twenty ten it was removed. So in these algorithms it has one indication: symptomatic bradycardia, in a patient who has a pulse.

The dose has changed, and this is an old-versus-new trap. It used to be half a milligram. Since twenty twenty the American dose is one milligram, repeated every three to five minutes, to a maximum of three milligrams, which is three doses. The European guideline still gives half a milligram, to the same maximum, so in an American-style question half a milligram is the old answer. Doses that are too small can slow the heart further, a paradoxical effect.

[[Atropine is for symptomatic bradycardia only, never for arrest: one milligram every three to five minutes, to a maximum of three milligrams. Half a milligram is the older American dose.]]

If it fails, the next steps are transcutaneous pacing, or an infusion of adrenaline or dopamine.

Now where it works and where it doesn't, which you met in the rhythm packet. Atropine blocks the vagus, and the vagus supplies the sinus node and the AV node. So a block at the node responds: a narrow escape rhythm, Mobitz one, an inferior infarct. A block below the node has no vagal supply to remove: a wide escape rhythm, Mobitz two, an anterior infarct. And a transplanted heart has no nerves at all. In those, you go to pacing.

The exam's point is that you still start with atropine while the pacing is being set up. The Grand Test stem was a heart rate of thirty-four, a pressure of eighty over fifty, complete heart block and good contractility. Only twenty-two per cent chose atropine. The popular wrong options were a permanent pacemaker and cardioversion. A permanent device comes after the patient is stable, and cardioversion is for a tachycardia.

The NEET recall was a bradycardia of forty-two after stenting for an acute coronary syndrome: the drug to start is atropine. Dopamine and noradrenaline, offered beside it, are the second line.

[[Unstable bradycardia, even complete heart block: atropine first while pacing is prepared. If the block is below the node, expect it to fail and pace.]]

steps.bridge: Route settled. One card now gathers the whole drug plan onto a single page, and adds what the bank asked.

lesson.text:
Every drug so far assumed a line. So which line?

In an adult arrest, attempt intravenous access first. If that fails or isn't feasible, intraosseous access is reasonable. That order is a change in twenty twenty-five, and it rests on trials. For years the intraosseous needle was promoted as the faster first choice. Then large randomised trials compared an intraosseous-first strategy with an intravenous-first one in arrests outside hospital: PARAMEDIC three in Britain and IVIO in Denmark. A third, from Taiwan, was later retracted, and the two that stand tell the same story. The intraosseous route gave no better survival or neurological outcome, and in the pooled analysis the odds of sustained ROSC were lower. A drug given into the tibia probably reaches the heart more slowly.

[[Adult arrest: try intravenous access first, and go intraosseous if it fails. An intraosseous-first strategy did not improve outcomes and lowered the odds of sustained ROSC.]]

So 'intraosseous first because it is faster' is now a wrong option in arrest.

The tracheal route is the second change. Older teaching allowed adrenaline down the tube, at two to two and a half times the intravenous dose, diluted in five to ten millilitres. Blood levels by that route are low and unpredictable, and the guideline of twenty twenty-five has removed it. Marrow still keys 'adrenaline can be given intratracheally' as a true statement. Choose it only when the question is plainly an old one and nothing better is offered.

Now move the same needle to a different patient, because the bank does. A trauma patient is in haemorrhagic shock, and two attempts at a peripheral line have failed. Next step? Eighty-one per cent got it: an intraosseous needle, in the proximal humerus or the tibia. It delivers drugs, fluid and blood within a minute. The wrong option is a subclavian or jugular line, which takes longer and risks a pneumothorax in a collapsed patient. The working rule is two failed attempts, or about ninety seconds.

That patient may be awake. And here is the question you missed in Grand Test eight.

The needle going through the bone is not the worst part. The pain comes when you infuse. The marrow is a rigid, closed space with its own pressure-sensitive nerve fibres, and a flush raises the pressure inside it sharply. Skin anaesthetic doesn't touch that. So in a conscious patient you anaesthetise the marrow itself, through the needle, before you flush.

The drug is lidocaine, two per cent, free of preservative and with no adrenaline in it. The dose is forty milligrams, which is two millilitres, given slowly over two minutes. Let it dwell for about a minute. Then flush with five to ten millilitres of saline. If pain returns, a further twenty milligrams.

[[Before flushing or infusing through an intraosseous line in a conscious patient, give forty milligrams of two per cent lidocaine slowly into the marrow, wait a minute, then flush. This was a Grand Test eight miss.]]

Notice that lidocaine has now appeared twice in this section, at two different doses. As an antiarrhythmic in refractory VF, it is one to one point five milligrams per kilogram into the circulation. As an anaesthetic for the marrow, it is a flat forty milligrams.

And know where the needle must not go: a fractured bone, a bone that has already had an intraosseous needle, an infected site, and osteogenesis imperfecta.

steps.bridge: Drugs and shocks treat the rhythm. But a heart in PEA has a normal rhythm. What stopped it?

lesson.text:
This card is the whole drug plan on one page, so use it to check what you now hold.

Shockable rhythm: adrenaline one milligram after the second shock, then every three to five minutes. Amiodarone three hundred milligrams, then a hundred and fifty, or lidocaine. Non-shockable rhythm: adrenaline as soon as possible. No shock, and no amiodarone.

Three bank stems hang on those lines. A monitor shows an organised rhythm at seventy-six a minute, and there is no pulse. Sixty-one per cent gave adrenaline. The wrong options were a shock and amiodarone. A rate of seventy-six looks reassuring, but without a pulse it is PEA. Second: refractory VF with no amiodarone on the trolley. The alternative is lidocaine, and sixty-five per cent knew it. Third, the child's dose of lidocaine, where only half were right. It is one milligram per kilogram. The wrong option is nought point one. Adrenaline is the one with the small decimal, nought point nought one.

{{**Arrest drug | Adult | Child**
Adrenaline | 1 mg every 3–5 min | 0.01 mg/kg
Amiodarone | 300 mg, then 150 mg | 5 mg/kg (up to 3 doses)
Lidocaine | 1–1.5, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg | 1 mg/kg}}

Now something Marrow asks about lidocaine that isn't an arrest question at all. A patient is in atrial fibrillation: which drug can't be used? Lignocaine. Class one B drugs, lidocaine and mexiletine, work only on ventricular arrhythmias. They bind the sodium channel during the long plateau of the ventricular action potential. The atrial action potential is too short to give them time. They are also the one class that shortens the QT.

[[Lidocaine is class one B: it acts only on ventricular tissue, is useless in atrial fibrillation, and shortens the QT. In a child the arrest dose is one milligram per kilogram.]]

A word on what adrenaline achieves, so that you hold it honestly. In PARAMEDIC two, about eight thousand arrests outside hospital were given adrenaline or placebo. Thirty-day survival was a little better with adrenaline, but more of the survivors had severe neurological disability. It restarts hearts. It doesn't protect brains.

Last, the part of the card on refractory VF. What really matters there is not another drug. It is the quality of CPR, meaning depth, rate, recoil and short pauses, and standard shocks. Two newer ideas are changing the pad position, called vector change, and firing two defibrillators in quick succession, called double sequential defibrillation. One trial, DOSE-VF in twenty twenty-two, found more survivors with both, around thirty per cent with double sequential shocks against thirteen with standard ones. But it was a single, small trial. So the guideline of twenty twenty-five says their usefulness is not established.

[[In refractory VF, CPR quality and standard shocks matter most. Double sequential defibrillation and vector change are not established. Vasopressin, routine calcium and routine bicarbonate add nothing.]]

steps.bridge: Suppose the cause is fixed and the heart restarts. How does the team know, without stopping to check?

lesson.text:
Shocks and drugs treat the rhythm. But many arrests aren't a rhythm problem. Something outside the conduction system has stopped the heart, and until that is found, nothing else will work. This matters most in PEA, where the rhythm is already organised.

The list is the five H's and the five T's. Learn each one by how it stops the heart.

The H's. Hypovolaemia: no filling. Hypoxia: no oxygen for the muscle. Hydrogen ion, meaning acidosis, which weakens contraction and blunts the response to adrenaline. Potassium, too low or too high, which destabilises the resting membrane. And hypothermia, which slows conduction and invites fibrillation.

The T's. Tension pneumothorax and cardiac tamponade, which are both obstruction: the heart can't fill, so compressions move nothing until the pressure is let out. Toxins. And thrombosis twice, in the lung and in a coronary artery.

{{**5 H's | 5 T's**
Hypovolaemia | Tension pneumothorax
Hypoxia | Tamponade
Hydrogen ion | Toxins
Hypo/hyperkalaemia | Thrombosis, pulmonary
Hypothermia | Thrombosis, coronary}}

The bank's easy version asks which is not on the list, and the answer is thrombocytopenia. It sounds like thrombosis, which is the point.

One clue helps you choose between them at the bedside. In PEA, look at the width of the complexes. Narrow and fast suggests a mechanical cause: tension, tamponade, bleeding, a pulmonary embolus. Broad and slow suggests a metabolic or toxic one: high potassium, acidosis, a sodium-channel blocker.

Now tension pneumothorax, the Marrow question. A ventilated patient on a PEEP of twenty goes into PEA, with absent breath sounds on the left and a shifted trachea. In an arrested, ventilated patient the signs are one silent side, rising airway pressures, and tracheal deviation late. The answer is immediate decompression, by needle or by finger thoracostomy, and then a chest drain. The wrong option is a chest X-ray to confirm it.

[[Tension pneumothorax in arrest is decompressed on clinical signs alone, by needle or finger, with no imaging first. Then a chest drain.]]

Next, a harder question, at forty-nine per cent. Which electrolyte disturbance is least likely to cause arrest in pregnancy? The answer is hypernatraemia. The electrolytes that stop a heart are potassium, calcium and magnesium. Low calcium lengthens the QT. Low magnesium triggers torsades. High magnesium, from an infusion for pre-eclampsia, blocks conduction. Sodium harms the brain, not the rhythm.

Last, a note your card carries from twenty twenty-five. In an arrest from suspected hyperkalaemia, the effectiveness of intravenous calcium is not well established, and the same is said of bicarbonate and of insulin with glucose. They may be given, but they must never push aside CPR, shocks and adrenaline. Don't over-read this. In a patient with a pulse, high potassium and ECG changes, calcium is still the first drug and still the exam's answer. The doubt applies only once the heart has stopped.

[[The electrolytes that stop the heart are potassium, calcium and magnesium, not sodium. In a hyperkalaemic arrest, calcium may be given but its benefit is unproven, and it must not displace CPR and adrenaline.]]

steps.bridge: That is the arrest that ends well. The last card of this section is the one that doesn't: when do you stop?

lesson.text:
You can't keep stopping compressions to feel for a pulse. So the return of a circulation has to announce itself on the monitors while your hands are still working. There are three signs.

The first is on the capnograph, and you have its mechanism already. The heart starts, the output jumps, and the carbon dioxide stored in the tissues during the low-flow state is washed to the lungs. The end-tidal rises abruptly and stays up. Classically that is to forty millimetres of mercury or more. The text of twenty twenty-five says a sudden rise of more than ten.

The word that matters is abrupt. A slow climb from fifteen to twenty-two means the compressions are getting better. It doesn't mean ROSC. ROSC is a step, not a slope. And a rise just after bicarbonate is the buffer releasing carbon dioxide.

The second sign needs an arterial line: spontaneous pressure waves appearing between your compressions, or a sudden rise in the diastolic pressure. The heart is ejecting on its own.

The third is the confirmation: a palpable pulse and a measurable blood pressure. That one needs a pause, so you look for it at the two-minute rhythm check, not before.

[[ROSC shows as an abrupt, sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide, or as spontaneous arterial waves, and is confirmed by a pulse and a blood pressure at the rhythm check. A gradual rise only means better compressions.]]

steps.bridge: Those are the rules for the ordinary arrest. Some arrests break them. Section four is about those.

lesson.text:
Sometimes nothing works. Then the question is who may stop, and on what grounds, without relying on one person's feeling in the back of an ambulance. The answer is a set of termination of resuscitation rules, built from registries of arrests outside hospital.

The one the Grand Tests have asked twice is the universal rule. It has three criteria, and all three must be present. The arrest was not witnessed by the EMS crew. No shock was delivered at any point. And there was no return of spontaneous circulation.

Look at what those three say together. Nobody professional saw the collapse, so it had already lasted an unknown time. The rhythm was never shockable, so it was never the kind that responds best. And nothing has worked. Survival in that group is very low.

[[Universal termination rule, all three: arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC. It is the rule for a tiered EMS system with both basic and advanced crews.]]

Which rule applies depends on what the crew is allowed to do. The basic life support rule uses the same three criteria. The advanced life support rule adds two more: the arrest was not witnessed by a bystander, and no bystander gave CPR. So it is the stricter rule, because an advanced crew can offer more. A note on your card had this backwards. For the exam, hold on to one line: a tiered system with both kinds of crew uses the universal rule.

Now the measurement that must not be used alone, and it is the trap in this card. You saw that a low end-tidal carbon dioxide means poor flow. It is tempting to turn that into a stopping rule. The guideline allows it only in a narrow form. In an intubated patient, an end-tidal that has failed to rise above ten millimetres of mercury after twenty minutes of advanced life support may be one part of a wider judgement. In a patient who is not intubated, no end-tidal cut-off should be used at all, because a leaking mask makes the number unreliable.

[[End-tidal carbon dioxide is never used alone to stop a resuscitation. Under ten after twenty minutes counts only in an intubated patient, and only as one factor among several.]]

When a rule is met, crews should be prepared to stop at the scene, and they need training in telling a family about a death. Transporting a patient with CPR in progress is dangerous for the crew and seldom saves anyone who meets the rule.

One boundary. These rules were built for medical arrests outside hospital. They are not validated for trauma, for overdose, or for arrests in hospital. Trauma has its own logic, and Marrow asked it. A resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating trauma with less than about fifteen minutes of CPR, or blunt trauma with less than about ten. A man with a penetrating chest wound in asystole after twenty-five minutes is outside that window. The answer is an echo, and with no cardiac motion, to stop.

spine: Adrenaline 1 mg = 10 mL of 1:10,000 every 3–5 min: at once in asystole/PEA, after the 2nd shock in VF/pVT. Same in pregnancy. Vasopressin: no advantage.
Refractory VF: amiodarone 300 → 150 mg OR lidocaine 1–1.5 → 0.5–0.75 mg/kg (ALPS: equal). Lidocaine = class Ib, ventricular only, shortens QT.
Atropine: bradycardia only, 1 mg × 3 (max 3 mg; 0.5 mg is old AHA, still ERC). Give it first even in complete block while pacing is set up.
Access: IV first, IO if it fails (2025); ET route removed. Trauma with 2 failed IVs → IO. Conscious patient: 40 mg 2% lidocaine into the marrow before flushing.
PEA: hunt the 5 H's and 5 T's. Narrow = mechanical, broad = metabolic/toxic. Tension: decompress without imaging. Hypernatraemia does not stop the heart.
ROSC = abrupt sustained ETCO₂ rise. Universal TOR: not EMS-witnessed + no shock + no ROSC. Never stop on ETCO₂ alone; rules don't apply to trauma.

open.text:
So far you have used two tools: hands and electricity. Now the syringe. Be honest about what drugs do in an arrest. They raise the chance of getting a pulse back. None of them has been shown to raise the number of patients who leave hospital with a good brain. That is why drugs come after compressions and shocks, and never instead of them.

This section answers four questions in order. Which drug, when, and at what dose? By which route? What caused this arrest, and can it be reversed? And when is it right to stop?

Listen for two kinds of trap. The first is old numbers: half a milligram of atropine, vasopressin as a substitute, the drug squirted down the tracheal tube. All three have gone. The second is arithmetic. The commonest error in this section is a tenfold one, made while drawing up adrenaline.

[[Arrest drugs support compressions and shocks; they never replace them. Adrenaline is the only vasopressor, and it is given by vein first.]]

One of your Grand Test misses lives here too: the intraosseous line in a patient who is awake.

Begin with the drug every arrest receives.

questions.text: Special arrests: pregnancy, asthma, poisoning, ECPR

steps.bridge: Displacement and an expert airway are the two priorities. The algorithm adds a short list of further changes.

lesson.text:
Compressions push forward only what has returned to the heart. Now put a uterus on the inferior vena cava.

From about twenty weeks, when the fundus reaches the umbilicus, a woman lying flat has her vena cava and her aorta compressed by the uterus. Much of the venous return from the lower body never reaches the heart. You can compress perfectly, and there is little in the ventricle to move. So maternal arrest has two priorities instead of one: high-quality CPR, and relief of aortocaval compression.

The relief is manual. Someone pushes or pulls the uterus up and to the left, continuously, while the woman stays flat on her back. Why not tilt her on a wedge, as was done before? Because a tilted chest takes the force out of the compressions. Manual left uterine displacement keeps her flat for good compressions and still lifts the uterus off the cava.

[[In maternal arrest, from about twenty weeks, add continuous manual left uterine displacement with the woman flat. Tilting her weakens compressions. This is the most critical change to standard life support.]]

The bank asked it at twenty-eight weeks, and ninety-seven per cent got it. NEET's own version is subtler: why is a second rescuer essential in maternal arrest? For uterine displacement. The wrong options are 'for the caesarean' and 'for defibrillation'. The second pair of hands is holding the uterus.

Now the airway, and why it is worse here. The mucosa is swollen, so the view is poor and it bleeds. The stomach is full, and the sphincter above it is lax, so she aspirates easily. Her reserve of oxygen in the lungs is smaller and she uses oxygen faster, so she desaturates quickly. So a difficult airway is common, and the most experienced person available should manage it.

Which device? The bank asked for the preferred airway in maternal arrest, and ninety-two per cent chose the endotracheal tube, because a cuffed tube protects best against aspiration. A supraglottic airway is the alternative. Either is confirmed with waveform capnography. Once it is in, the rate is what you already know: one breath every six seconds with continuous compressions.

Two wrong options to recognise. 'Half-dose adrenaline in pregnancy' is wrong, because the doses don't change. 'Avoid intubation until ROSC' is wrong, because the airway is secured early.

And the team is larger from the first minute: obstetrics, the neonatal team, anaesthesia, intensive care. You'll see why two cards from now.

steps.bridge: If displacement, calcium and blood haven't restored a pulse, one obstacle remains, and it can be removed.

lesson.text:
The maternal algorithm adds a short list to standard life support. Take the maternal changes first, then the obstetric ones, then the causes.

First, where the cannula goes. With the cava compressed, a drug injected into a leg vein may sit below the obstruction and never reach the heart. So access is placed above the diaphragm, in an arm, or intraosseous in the humerus.

Second, oxygen at a hundred per cent, and no excessive ventilation, for the reasons you know.

Third, magnesium. Many of these women are on a magnesium infusion for pre-eclampsia. Magnesium in excess abolishes the reflexes, depresses breathing, blocks conduction and stops the heart. So in a woman who arrests on a magnesium infusion, you stop the infusion and give calcium, as the chloride or the gluconate, which opposes magnesium at the cell membrane.

[[A woman who arrests while on a magnesium infusion: stop the magnesium and give intravenous calcium. Before the arrest magnesium is the treatment; during it, magnesium is a suspect.]]

The bank has three questions on this, and you need to keep them apart.

One: a pregnant woman in the ICU becomes bradycardic and then arrests. Which electrolyte? Hypermagnesaemia. Sixty-one per cent got it. The wrong options were low potassium and high calcium.

Two: arrest on intravenous magnesium for pre-eclampsia, with CPR and displacement already under way. Next step? Stop the magnesium and give calcium.

Three is different. Earlier you met the eclamptic woman who was seizing and went into VF, and the key gave magnesium with amiodarone. So here is the rule. If she was already receiving magnesium when she arrested, the answer is calcium. If she is eclamptic and has not been loaded, magnesium appears in the keyed answer.

Now the obstetric changes. There are three: continuous uterine displacement, detaching the fetal monitors, and preparing for delivery. Why take the monitors off? They get in the way of defibrillation and of the move to delivery, and they tell you nothing you can act on. The fetus is best served by getting the mother's circulation back. Marrow asked which step is not indicated in maternal arrest, and the answer was attaching fetal monitors.

Last, the causes, as an alphabet from A to H. Anaesthetic complications. Bleeding. Cardiovascular. Drugs. Embolic. Fever. General causes, which are the ordinary H's and T's. And hypertension.

{{**Maternal arrest: causes A–H**
**A**naesthetic complications • **B**leeding • **C**ardiovascular • **D**rugs (magnesium, local anaesthetic) • **E**mbolic (amniotic fluid, pulmonary) • **F**ever • **G**eneral H's and T's • **H**ypertension}}

One of them outweighs the rest. Obstetric haemorrhage is the commonest single cause of maternal arrest. So the bank's question, the commonest reversible cause of PEA in pregnancy, is answered by hypovolaemia from haemorrhage. That means wide lines above the diaphragm, a massive transfusion, drugs to contract the uterus, and the obstetrician. Eclampsia on its own seldom stops the heart.

[[PEA in pregnancy is hypovolaemia from obstetric haemorrhage until proved otherwise. Access goes above the diaphragm, and the fetal monitors come off.]]

steps.bridge: That was an obstacle to filling. The next arrests are defeated by gas and by temperature.

lesson.text:
You have pushed the uterus aside by hand. If that isn't enough, you empty it.

Start with the name, because it changed in twenty twenty-five. What used to be called perimortem caesarean delivery is now resuscitative delivery. The old name suggested an operation done at the point of death to rescue the baby. The new one says what it is: a step in the mother's resuscitation. Emptying the uterus releases the vena cava, returns blood from the uterine circulation to hers, and makes her chest easier to compress and to ventilate.
