In the case series, the mother's pulse often came back just after delivery.

Now the clock. Preparation begins the moment the arrest is recognised. That is why the obstetric and neonatal teams were called in the first minute. The goal is delivery completed by five minutes, if there is no ROSC, in a woman whose fundus is at or above the umbilicus.

[[Resuscitative delivery, the new name for perimortem caesarean: prepare when the arrest is recognised, and complete delivery by five minutes if there is no ROSC. It is done to resuscitate the mother.]]

Where does five minutes come from? From Katz, Dotters and Droegemueller in nineteen eighty-six. They reasoned that the brain tolerates about four to five minutes without flow, so they proposed starting the operation at four minutes and delivering by five. That is the four-minute rule. It is a goal drawn from case reports, and the reviews that followed, by Katz in two thousand and five and Einav in twenty twelve, were case series as well. There has never been a randomised trial.

The bank tests this three ways. Timing at thirty-four weeks: within five minutes of the arrest if there is no ROSC. Ninety-two per cent. The wrong options are 'after twenty minutes of failed CPR', 'only after fetal death' and 'after ROSC'.

The origin of the four-minute rule: Katz. Fifty-four per cent.

And one question with a bad key, which only fourteen per cent matched. It asked which trial studied maternal arrest and perimortem caesarean, and the key was something called the HELP trial. No such trial exists. If Katz or a case series is among the options, choose it. If the same options return, eliminate the ones you can identify. MOMS was fetal surgery for spina bifida. ALPS, in obstetrics, was steroids for late preterm birth. PROWESS was a sepsis drug. What is left is the key.

The operation is done where she lies, with CPR and displacement continuing. You don't move her to theatre. The bank asked the incision, and only forty-five per cent knew it. It is a vertical midline incision from just above the pubic symphysis up to the umbilicus, because that is the fastest and gives the widest view, and then a vertical cut in the uterus. The wrong options begin above the umbilicus or at the xiphoid, and those miss the uterus.

[[Resuscitative delivery is done at the bedside during CPR, through a vertical midline incision from just above the symphysis pubis to the umbilicus.]]

Two more recommendations from twenty twenty-five. If she doesn't respond to standard resuscitation, extracorporeal CPR is reasonable. These are young patients with reversible causes, and in the reported series most of them survived. And for suspected amniotic fluid embolism, where sudden collapse with right heart failure is followed by consumptive coagulopathy and torrential bleeding, use a massive transfusion protocol with a balanced ratio of products, together with tranexamic acid.

steps.bridge: Extracorporeal rewarming is the top of a ladder. The bank asks the rungs below it, and the rules for a cold arrest.

lesson.text:
Three conditions share this card because the guideline of twenty twenty-five gave each a physical answer.

First, asthma. Life-threatening asthma doesn't kill through damaged lung. It kills through gas that can't get out. Each breath stacks on the one before, the chest over-inflates, the pressure inside rises, and venous return is squeezed off. So in an asthmatic who arrests on a ventilator, think of two things at once: breath stacking, relieved by disconnecting the circuit briefly and letting the chest empty, and a tension pneumothorax. When the bronchospasm itself won't yield to standard treatment, two rescues are named. Extracorporeal life support may be reasonable, because it takes over gas exchange and buys time for the bronchodilators. And volatile anaesthetics may be considered, because they relax bronchial smooth muscle directly. Survival in the observational series is high, eighty-three to a hundred per cent, because the disease is reversible.

Second, heat. Heat stroke is a core temperature above forty degrees with brain dysfunction. The injury to cells depends on how long they stay above the critical temperature. So the only thing that matters is the speed at which the core falls.

Water carries heat away far faster than air. So the preferred method is immersion in ice water, at one to five degrees. The target is to cool as fast as possible, at a rate of at least nought point one five of a degree per minute. If ice water isn't available, tepid water or ice water held in a tarpaulin is the next choice. Evaporative cooling with ice packs is the fallback when immersion is impossible.

[[Heat stroke: immersion in ice water, cooling at least nought point one five of a degree per minute, and stop at about thirty-eight point six degrees. Antipyretics and dantrolene do nothing.]]

Why do antipyretics fail? Because this isn't fever. In fever the hypothalamus has raised its set-point, and paracetamol lowers it. In heat stroke the set-point is normal and the body simply can't shed the heat. Dantrolene belongs to malignant hyperthermia only.

The bank asked the first step twice. A hot day, a core of forty-one, confusion: ice-water immersion. The wrong options were cooling blankets with fans, and cold intravenous fluid alone.

And here is the wrong key. A question on exertional heat stroke was keyed 'cool to at least thirty-six degrees to prevent rebound', and seventy-eight per cent chose it. That is too far. You stop active cooling at about thirty-eight point six to thirty-nine, because the core goes on falling after the patient leaves the water. If 'stop at thirty-nine' is offered, choose it.

Third, cold, at its severe end. Below twenty-eight degrees the heart fibrillates easily and doesn't respond well to anything until it is warm. The best way to warm it is from the inside, with the circulation supported at the same time. So for a hypothermic arrest the recommendation is rewarming with extracorporeal life support. It may also be used for a core below twenty-eight degrees even without an arrest.

Who should be offered it? Not everyone found cold is alive. The guideline says to use a prognostic score, HOPE or ICE, to decide. HOPE gives a probability of survival, and under ten per cent argues against starting.

[[Hypothermic arrest: rewarm with extracorporeal life support, with the HOPE or ICE score guiding who is cannulated. A core below twenty-eight degrees can be rewarmed this way even without arrest.]]

steps.bridge: Extracorporeal support has now rescued the mother, the asthmatic and the cold. What is it, and who gets it?

lesson.text:
This is a new card, because the bank asked hypothermia in ways your deck couldn't answer. Three grades, three ways of rewarming, and then the rules for the arrest.

The grades run by core temperature, and the rewarming becomes more invasive as the patient loses the ability to warm himself.

Mild is thirty-two to thirty-five degrees. This patient is still shivering, and shivering is a furnace: it raises the core by a degree or two an hour. So all he needs is passive external rewarming. Take off the wet clothes, insulate him, and warm the room.

Moderate is twenty-eight to thirty-two. Shivering has stopped, so he can't rewarm himself. He needs active external rewarming, with forced warm air, and intravenous fluid warmed to about forty degrees. Fluid at room temperature cools him.

Severe is below twenty-eight, or any cold patient who is unstable or arrested. He needs active internal rewarming: extracorporeal support first, and warm lavage of the chest or the peritoneum where that isn't available.

{{**Grade | Core | Rewarming**
Mild | 32–35 °C | passive external: dry, insulate
Moderate | 28–32 °C | active external (forced air) + fluid at 38–42 °C
Severe, unstable, arrest | <28 °C | active internal: ECLS; lavage if not}}

The question that caught people, at forty-seven per cent, treated passive rewarming as inadequate for mild hypothermia. It isn't. For a stable patient with mild hypothermia it is the answer. And a patient at thirty degrees with Osborn waves and a wide QRS is unstable, so the answer there was active internal rewarming with gentle handling.

Gentle, because the cold heart is irritable. Marrow asked which site hypothermia depresses first: the sinoatrial node. So the sequence is sinus bradycardia, then atrial fibrillation, then the Osborn or J wave with long intervals, and then ventricular fibrillation, most likely below twenty-eight degrees. Rough handling can provoke it. So the patient is moved gently and kept horizontal.

Now the arrest. A cold myocardium doesn't respond to shocks or drugs, and drugs given into a slow circulation pile up and arrive together on rewarming. So below thirty degrees you hold back.

[[Hypothermic arrest below thirty degrees: continue CPR and rewarm, limit the shocks, and withhold adrenaline and antiarrhythmics until the core is above thirty. Europe allows three shocks; America, since twenty twenty-five, one.]]

The detail differs by guideline. The European rule is up to three shocks, then no more until the core passes thirty, with no adrenaline below thirty and a doubled interval, every six to ten minutes, between thirty and thirty-five. The American rule of twenty twenty-five is one shock and then defer further shocks and adrenaline until thirty degrees. The older American position let you run the standard algorithm, and some banks still say America is the more permissive. That is out of date.

The bank's stem was VF at a core of twenty-nine. Fifty-three per cent got it: continue CPR and withhold antiarrhythmics until above thirty. Lidocaine doesn't work in a cold heart.

Last, when to stop. Cold protects the brain, so these resuscitations run long, and fixed pupils or Osborn waves tell you nothing about outcome. What does? Marrow asked which test decides whether to continue in a pulseless patient found in snow. Serum potassium. Above twelve millimoles per litre, the cells had already died and burst before the body cooled.

[[In a hypothermic arrest a serum potassium above twelve millimoles per litre means death came before cooling: stop, and do not start extracorporeal support. Fixed pupils do not count.]]

steps.bridge: ECPR only helps if the cause can be fixed. The commonest fixable cause of an adult arrest is a blocked coronary.

lesson.text:
Extracorporeal CPR means starting ECMO during an arrest that hasn't responded to conventional resuscitation. It doesn't treat anything. It replaces the circulation, so that the brain is perfused while somebody fixes the cause.

The configuration is always venoarterial. Think about why. In venovenous ECMO, oxygenated blood is returned to a vein and relies on the patient's own heart to send it round. This heart is still. Only blood returned to an artery perfuses anything.

[[ECPR is venoarterial ECMO, always, because there is no cardiac output to carry venous return forward. It buys time for a reversible cause; it does not treat one.]]

Who is a candidate? Every criterion answers one of two questions: was the brain without flow for only a short time, and is there something to fix? So: a witnessed arrest, with bystander CPR. An initial shockable rhythm, or another reversible cause. A younger patient with few other illnesses. And a definitive treatment standing ready: angioplasty, thrombectomy, rewarming.

The clock is the low-flow time, the time spent on conventional CPR. Most programmes aim to have the patient on the circuit within sixty minutes of the arrest.

The exclusions are the mirror image, plus three mechanical ones. An unwitnessed arrest. A long period with no CPR. A terminal illness. Then severe aortic regurgitation, because blood pumped backwards up the aorta pours through the leaking valve and distends the ventricle. Uncontrolled bleeding, because the circuit needs heparin. And aortic dissection.

What is the evidence? Three trials, and they disagree for a reason. ARREST, in Minneapolis, took thirty patients with refractory VF into a highly practised system, and survival to discharge was forty-three per cent against seven. It was stopped early. The Prague trial, with two hundred and sixty-four patients, found thirty-one per cent against twenty-two for good neurological survival, which was not significant. INCEPTION, across ten Dutch centres, found twenty against sixteen, also not significant. So the benefit appears only in fast, experienced systems, and the guideline calls ECPR reasonable in selected patients within a trained and equipped system.

Now the Grand Test question, which only forty-two per cent got right. It quoted the Surugadai criteria from Tokyo and asked which is not an exclusion. Four were offered: a presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within ten minutes of arrival, a core temperature under thirty-five degrees, and pregnancy. The answer is the core temperature under thirty-five. The true exclusion in those criteria is a core under thirty. A patient at thirty to thirty-five is mildly cold, and that is protective.

[[Surugadai ECPR exclusions: presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within ten minutes of arrival, core temperature below thirty degrees, and pregnancy. A core of thirty to thirty-five is not an exclusion.]]

Notice that ROSC within ten minutes is an exclusion and not a reason to cannulate. A patient who has a pulse no longer has a refractory arrest.

steps.bridge: The pulse is back. The arrest is over, and the illness that follows it is about to begin.

lesson.text:
Most sudden arrests in adults begin in a coronary artery. So the arrest algorithms carry the first page of the ACS pathway with them. You studied this in the two ACS packets, so here is only the route, and the one bank question.

It starts before hospital. Support the airway, breathing and circulation, monitor, and record a twelve-lead ECG, because an ECG sent ahead lets the catheter laboratory be activated before the patient arrives. Give aspirin. Consider a nitrate, and morphine only if the nitrate doesn't settle the pain. Transfer to a centre that can do emergency PCI.

In the emergency department, the assessment runs in parallel and inside ten minutes: vital signs, the twelve-lead ECG, a targeted history, high-sensitivity troponin, electrolytes and coagulation.

Aspirin is a hundred and sixty-two to three hundred and twenty-five milligrams, chewed, because chewing is absorbed faster. Oxygen is given only if the saturation is below ninety per cent. Nitrates are avoided in hypotension, in right ventricular infarction, and after a phosphodiesterase inhibitor.

Then the ECG splits the road. ST elevation, or a new left bundle branch block with a fitting story, is suspected STEMI. The instruction on the algorithm is: don't delay reperfusion. No ST elevation is a suspected non-ST-elevation syndrome. Troponin is taken on arrival. If it is positive and the picture fits, the patient goes to a monitored bed. If it is negative, it is repeated at one hour or at three hours, with monitoring in between.

[[Suspected ACS: a twelve-lead ECG within ten minutes decides everything. ST elevation goes to reperfusion without delay. The rest get monitoring, chewed aspirin and a repeat high-sensitivity troponin at one or three hours.]]

The Grand Test question had only forty-four per cent right. New chest pain with T wave inversion in the lateral leads: what is the most immediate step? Monitoring, oxygen if needed, and aspirin. NEET's favourite wrong option was to call the catheter laboratory for immediate PCI. T inversion isn't ST elevation. Immediate angiography without ST elevation is kept for the very high-risk patient: shock, pain that won't settle, an arrhythmia, a mechanical complication. The other wrong options gave two nitrates and watched, or sent the patient for a chest X-ray before the aspirin.

So the cause has been found and treated, or the shock has worked, or the adrenaline has. The capnograph jumps.

spine: Maternal arrest ≥20 weeks: CPR + continuous manual left uterine displacement (the 2nd rescuer's job); ETT by the most experienced; same drugs and energy.
IV above the diaphragm; on magnesium → stop it, give calcium; detach fetal monitors. PEA in pregnancy = obstetric haemorrhage first. Causes A–H.
Resuscitative delivery (was perimortem caesarean): prepare at recognition, deliver by 5 min; Katz 1986; vertical midline incision from above the symphysis.
Asthma: ECLS, volatile agents. Heat stroke: ice-water immersion, ≥0.15 °C/min, stop ~38.6 °C. Hypothermic arrest: ECLS rewarming guided by HOPE/ICE.
Hypothermia: mild passive, moderate active external, <28 °C active internal. Arrest <30 °C: limit shocks, no drugs. K⁺ >12 = stop.
ECPR = VA ECMO for a reversible cause, on circuit within ~60 min; Surugadai excludes core <30 °C (not <35). ACS: ECG within 10 min splits the road.

open.text:
Everything so far was the standard arrest: one algorithm, the same for everyone. This section is about the arrests where that algorithm, followed faithfully, still fails, because something about the patient defeats it.

A uterus lying on the vena cava, so that compressions have nothing to pump. Lungs so full of trapped gas that the heart can't fill. A heart too cold to answer a drug or a shock. A body so hot that every minute of delay costs cells. In each case you keep the algorithm, and you add the one thing that removes the obstacle. Usually that thing is physical, not a drug.

[[In a special arrest the standard algorithm continues, and you add the one manoeuvre that removes what is defeating it: push the uterus aside, let the gas out, warm the cold, cool the hot.]]

The traps here are mostly renamed things and wrong keys. Perimortem caesarean has a new name and a five-minute clock. Magnesium is a treatment before the arrest and a suspect during it. And one keyed answer on heat stroke is simply wrong.

Begin with the pregnant patient.

steps.bridge: That is the route. Now the numbers that sit on it, all five on one card.

lesson.text:
The algorithm after ROSC is short, and it is worth seeing whole before you learn its numbers.

Step one is ROSC itself. Step two is the lungs: optimise ventilation and oxygenation. That means a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight per cent, an advanced airway if the patient needs one, waveform capnography, and no hyperventilation.

Step three is the circulation. Treat hypotension with a fluid bolus, a vasopressor infusion, and a search for a treatable cause. Your card writes the threshold as a systolic pressure under ninety, which is how the older algorithm drew it. The guideline of twenty twenty-five frames it as a mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five.

Then come the two questions.

The first is asked of a twelve-lead ECG. Is this a STEMI, or is an acute infarct strongly suspected? If yes, the patient goes for coronary reperfusion.

The second is asked of the patient. Does he follow commands? If no, you start temperature control. If yes, he goes on to advanced critical care without it.

Look at that second question closely, because it is the only entry criterion. A patient who doesn't follow commands has an injured brain, and temperature control exists to protect an injured brain. It doesn't matter whether the rhythm was VF or asystole, whether the arrest was in hospital or outside, or whether he is now stable.

[[Not following commands after ROSC is the only trigger for temperature control: any rhythm, any location, stable or not.]]

Marrow asked it plainly. VF arrest, ROSC, comatose, haemodynamically stable: which modality do you consider? Targeted temperature management. The wrong option is 'he is stable, so nothing further'. Another is 'temperature control only after VF', which is how it stood twenty years ago.

And the two branches don't compete. They run in parallel. A comatose patient with a STEMI gets both, the catheter laboratory and temperature control. An awake patient with a STEMI gets the laboratory only. A comatose patient with no ST elevation gets temperature control only.

steps.bridge: Two of those five targets are set at the ventilator. Take them properly, starting with the lungs.

lesson.text:
Five targets, and each one exists for the brain.

Blood pressure: a mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five millimetres of mercury. After an arrest the brain loses its autoregulation. Normally it holds its own flow steady across a range of pressures. Now its flow simply follows the pressure. So hypotension is a second ischaemic injury.

Oxygen: a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight per cent, which is an arterial oxygen tension of sixty to a hundred and five. Too little repeats the injury. Too much feeds free-radical damage in tissue that has just been reperfused. And you keep a hundred per cent oxygen running until the oximeter gives a reading you can trust, and titrate down only then.

Carbon dioxide: an arterial tension of thirty-five to forty-five. Carbon dioxide sets the calibre of the brain's vessels. Low constricts them and cuts flow to a brain that is already short of it. High dilates them and raises intracranial pressure.

Temperature: deliberate temperature control for at least thirty-six hours in any patient who doesn't follow commands, at a goal anywhere from thirty-two to thirty-seven point five degrees. The next section is spent on why that range is so wide. For now hold one thing: the part that matters is preventing fever.

Angiography: before discharge, in survivors where a cardiac cause is suspected, especially after a shockable rhythm, with unexplained left ventricular dysfunction, or with severe ischaemia. That is the non-urgent indication. The urgent one comes three cards from now.

{{**After ROSC (AHA 2025)**
MAP | ≥65 mmHg
SpO₂ | 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105 mmHg)
PaCO₂ | 35–45 mmHg
Temperature | 32–37.5 °C for ≥36 h, if not following commands
Glucose | avoid <70 and >180 mg/dL}}

[[After ROSC: mean arterial pressure at least sixty-five, saturation ninety to ninety-eight per cent, arterial carbon dioxide thirty-five to forty-five, and temperature control at thirty-two to thirty-seven point five degrees for at least thirty-six hours.]]

Now the trap that is built on history. A bank question asks for the target temperature after a VF arrest, and its key is thirty-two to thirty-four degrees. Only fifty-seven per cent chose it. That was the right answer from two thousand and two to about twenty ten. It isn't wrong inside today's range. It is just no longer the range. If thirty-two to thirty-seven point five, or fever prevention, is among the options, choose that. If only historical ranges are offered, thirty-two to thirty-four is the keyed one.

steps.bridge: The lungs are set. Now the pressure, where one keyed answer departs from every guideline.

lesson.text:
The lungs first, because they are set within minutes of ROSC and they control two of the five targets.

Two airway steps begin it. Secure the airway if the patient is not protecting it. And pass a gastric tube. During CPR the bag and mask filled the stomach with air, as you saw in the first section, and a distended stomach splints the diaphragm and invites aspiration.

Then ventilate protectively, with a tidal volume of about six to eight millilitres per kilogram of predicted body weight. These lungs have often aspirated, they have been compressed, and they are now being reperfused. Lung injury is common after arrest.

Then the two gases.

Carbon dioxide is held at thirty-five to forty-five, normal. Check it on a blood gas instead of trusting the capnograph, and check it again whenever the temperature changes. A cooled patient makes less carbon dioxide. Leave the ventilator as it was, and he drifts into a low carbon dioxide without anyone touching a dial.

Oxygen is held at a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight per cent. The lower limit moved in twenty twenty-five. It was ninety-two before, and the European guideline still says ninety-four. What allowed the wider range was the BOX trial, which compared a lower and a higher oxygen target in comatose survivors and found the same outcome with both. So the safe zone is broad, and the harm is at the two ends.

[[After ROSC ventilate to normal: arterial carbon dioxide thirty-five to forty-five, saturation ninety to ninety-eight per cent. Hyperventilation, hyperoxia and hypoxia each injure the brain by a different route.]]

Name those routes, because the exam asks what to avoid. Hyperventilation constricts the brain's vessels and also raises pressure in the chest, which lowers output. Hyperoxia adds free-radical injury. Hypoxia repeats the arrest in miniature.

The Grand Test asked it twice. A post-arrest patient on temperature management: which should be avoided? Fever, hypoxia, or hyperventilation? All of the above. Everyone got it. The wrong reasoning is that only fever matters during temperature control.

One discriminator, because you know another setting where hyperventilation is used. In a herniating brain, a short period of hyperventilation buys time by shrinking the blood volume in the skull. The brain after an arrest has the opposite problem. It is short of flow. So here hyperventilation is only harmful.

steps.bridge: Pressure is held. Now the first of the two questions: is there an artery to open?

lesson.text:
Now the circulation, and you have the tools for this from the two shock packets. After an arrest all three numbers can be off at once. The pump is stunned. The squeeze is lost, because reperfusion dilates the vessels. And the filling may be low. So you find out which is failing before you treat.

The lines come first: an arterial line, because vasopressors are titrated minute by minute, and a central line to deliver them. Then two investigations. A twelve-lead ECG, for the infarct. And an echo, which tells you which number is wrong: a poor ventricle, a vigorous ventricle with low resistance, or an obstruction such as tamponade or a dilated right ventricle.

The treatment follows the finding. Fluid only if the patient is volume-responsive, in small boluses, reassessed each time. The old fixed load of twenty to thirty millilitres per kilogram has gone, because a stunned ventricle can't handle it and the injured lung takes it up. For the vasopressor, noradrenaline is the usual first choice, with dobutamine when the stunned pump is the problem. Neither guideline claims one agent is proven. Mechanical support, a balloon pump, an Impella or ECMO, is not routine. It may be considered in selected patients with refractory cardiogenic shock.

Now the target. A mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five, with a urine output of half to one millilitre per kilogram an hour. The purpose is cerebral perfusion.

[[The post-arrest pressure target is a mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five. The BOX trial compared sixty-three with seventy-seven and found no difference, so a higher target has no guideline support.]]

That brings us to a question only twenty-four per cent matched. A comatose patient on temperature management, day one, with a mean pressure of sixty-five despite fluids. Next step? The key was to raise the mean pressure above eighty. The reasoning sounds sensible: a brain without autoregulation should like a higher pressure. But it was tested. BOX, in twenty twenty-two, assigned comatose survivors to a mean of sixty-three or seventy-seven and found no difference in death or severe disability. Three other trials agreed. No guideline asks for eighty.

So how do you answer? If that exact stem returns, with those options, the bank's key is above eighty. On a question framed by a guideline, the target is at least sixty-five. The European wording is a mean above sixty to sixty-five.

One discriminator stops this number from blurring with others. A mean of eighty-five to ninety belongs to acute spinal cord injury. Traumatic brain injury is managed by cerebral perfusion pressure. Neither applies after an arrest.

The other wrong options in that stem teach something too. 'Rewarm rapidly' causes rebound hypotension and fever. 'Stop temperature control because of a STEMI' is wrong, because the two run together. And 'delay reperfusion until he wakes' is wrong, for the reason on the next card.

[[After ROSC give fluid only if the patient is volume-responsive, noradrenaline first, and dobutamine for a stunned pump. Mechanical support is not routine.]]

steps.bridge: The artery is dealt with. Now the brain begins to show its injury, and often the first sign is a jerk.

lesson.text:
The first of the two questions: is there an artery to open?

Read the post-ROSC ECG. If it shows persistent ST elevation, the patient goes for emergent angiography, with PCI if a culprit is found. And the key phrase is 'comatose or not'. Coma is not a reason to wait.

That is where the Grand Test caught half the candidates. A man collapses in VF after shovelling snow. He has ROSC, his mental status can't be assessed, and the ECG shows a STEMI. When is angiography? Urgently, now. The wrong options were to wait for a favourable neurological prognosis, to correct the metabolic derangement first, and to go within twenty-four to forty-eight hours. Think about why waiting is wrong. You can't judge the brain's prognosis for at least three days. The muscle beyond the blocked artery dies in hours. And if the artery stays shut he may arrest again.

[[Persistent ST elevation after ROSC means emergent angiography, comatose or not. Temperature control starts alongside it and neither delays the other.]]

The NEET recall asked the same thing with instability added. VF arrest, ROSC, anterior ST elevation, unstable: immediate coronary angiography with PCI. The wrong option there is thrombolysis. Primary PCI is preferred, and prolonged or traumatic CPR raises the bleeding risk of a lytic. Lysis is kept for when PCI can't be reached in time.

Now the patient without ST elevation. This is where practice changed. It used to be argued that anyone resuscitated from VF with no obvious cause should go straight to the laboratory. Two trials tested that. COACT took about five hundred and fifty patients after a shockable arrest with no ST elevation. Survival at ninety days was sixty-five per cent with immediate angiography and sixty-seven with a delayed one. TOMAHAWK found no benefit either.

So without ST elevation, emergent angiography is reasonable only in three situations: cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias, or ongoing ischaemia. Otherwise it is not emergent, and it is done later, before discharge.

{{**Angiography after ROSC | When**
Persistent ST elevation (awake or comatose) | emergent
No STE + shock, recurrent VT/VF or ongoing ischaemia | emergent is reasonable
No STE, stable | delayed (COACT, TOMAHAWK)}}

[[Without ST elevation, immediate angiography adds nothing unless there is cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmia or ongoing ischaemia. 'No obvious cause' is no longer an indication.]]

Two more lines on the card. Temperature control can be started during the angiogram, on the table. And the medical treatment for ACS, antiplatelets, anticoagulation and a statin, is begun in appropriate patients, adjusted for the bleeding risk that CPR leaves behind.

Finally the arrhythmias that follow ROSC. They are mostly secondary, so you treat the cause more than the rhythm: correct the potassium and magnesium, reperfuse the ischaemia, deal with any toxin, and correct the temperature. Cooling produces bradycardia. Rewarming and fever produce tachyarrhythmias.

steps.bridge: One summary card pulls the first hours together, and adds a definition the exam can ask.

lesson.text:
Now the second question, the brain. Often the first thing it shows you is movement.

Seizures occur in about a third of patients who stay comatose after ROSC. Myoclonus is the commonest form, seen in about twenty to twenty-five per cent. Read your card carefully here. 'More common' means the commonest type of seizure activity, not more frequent than seizures as a whole. Many of the others are visible only on EEG.

Both are markers of severe injury. But there are two kinds of myoclonus after anoxia, and they mean opposite things.

The first is early status myoclonus: continuous, generalised jerks of the face and trunk within the first one to three days, in a patient who is comatose, with a malignant EEG such as burst suppression. That points to severe cortical damage and a poor outcome.

The second is the Lance-Adams syndrome: jerks brought on by action, appearing days to weeks later, in a patient who is waking up, with a near-normal EEG background. He survives, and the jerks themselves are his disability.

[[Early status myoclonus in a comatose patient with a malignant EEG signals a poor outcome. Lance-Adams myoclonus comes later, with action, in a patient who is awake, and carries a good outlook for survival.]]

The Grand Test stem was a woman rewarmed after twenty-four hours of hypothermia, with rapid twitching of the face and limbs and rhythmic activity on the EEG. Eighty-four per cent chose correctly: post-anoxic myoclonic status epilepticus indicates a poor prognosis. The wrong options are that EEG activity means a good chance of recovery, that a lumbar puncture is essential, and that oxcarbazepine and topiramate are the proven drugs. No drug is proven.

Now the management, in four rules.

One: no prophylaxis. Both guidelines advise against routine anticonvulsants, because no trial showed a benefit.

Two: get an EEG. It tells you whether the movement is a seizure, and it monitors the effect of treatment.

Three: treat real seizures. First line is levetiracetam or sodium valproate, usually with a sedative such as propofol. For myoclonus the drugs are propofol, valproate, clonazepam and levetiracetam. Phenytoin doesn't work for post-anoxic myoclonus.

Four, new in twenty twenty-five: don't treat myoclonus that has no EEG correlate. There is no evidence that those movements injure the brain further, and the sedatives needed to suppress them cloud the examination you will depend on for prognosis.

[[After ROSC: no seizure prophylaxis; EEG for any movement; levetiracetam or valproate first; phenytoin fails in myoclonus; and myoclonus with no EEG correlate is left untreated.]]

The second Grand Test question, at sixty-nine per cent. A comatose patient has a malignant epileptiform EEG that has persisted for ninety minutes on propofol and valproate. Next step? Add levetiracetam. The wrong options were to wait and to stop the sedation.

Hold one honest caveat alongside that. The TELSTAR trial, in twenty twenty-two, treated these rhythmic and periodic EEG patterns aggressively, and about nine in ten patients did badly whether the pattern was suppressed or not. So you escalate because seizure activity is running, not because it will rescue the prognosis.

And one mimic. A patient under temperature control who is moving rhythmically may be shivering. Shivering has no EEG change, and it settles when the skin is warmed.

steps.bridge: You hold the current targets. The exam mixes them with the previous set, so put the two side by side.

lesson.text:
This card is the first hours on one page, so check yourself against it.

Pressure: a mean of at least sixty-five. The card adds a systolic of at least ninety, which was the older pair. Gases: saturation ninety to ninety-eight, carbon dioxide thirty-five to forty-five. Temperature: thirty-two to thirty-seven point five, for any rhythm and any location, for at least thirty-six hours, with rewarming no faster than half a degree an hour. Angiography: at once for a STEMI, reasonable for shock, and not for everyone.

A Grand Test question you missed sits on the temperature line. The wrong options were a strict thirty-two to thirty-four degrees, excluding PEA from temperature control, and thirty-six degrees for twelve hours. Each is an old or an invented number. Any comatose survivor, any rhythm, at least thirty-six hours.

Now the one new item on this card, a definition. The EEG is watched in every patient who doesn't follow commands, and sometimes it shows seizures with no movement at all. When does that count as status epilepticus? When a seizure runs continuously for ten minutes or more, or when seizures occupy twenty per cent or more of any sixty minutes. That second half is twelve minutes in an hour.

[[Electrographic status epilepticus: a seizure lasting ten minutes or more continuously, or seizures filling twenty per cent or more of any sixty-minute period.]]

Marrow hangs three prognosis questions on this card, and they prepare you for the last section.

First: which finding in post-arrest coma is most specific for a poor outcome? Status epilepticus, or myoclonic status, during temperature control. It stands with the other poor signs: pupillary and corneal reflexes absent on both sides, a high neurone-specific enolase, and burst suppression on the EEG. All of them are read together, and not before seventy-two hours.

Second: a man is revived after a twenty-minute arrest, and you are asked which statement is not true. The false one is that no motor response in the upper limbs always means a poor outcome. Arms that are weak while the legs move can be a watershed injury, called man in a barrel. The border zones between the cerebral arteries are the last fields to be supplied when pressure falls, and the arm area of the motor cortex lies in one. It doesn't always mean a poor outcome.

Third: a brief arrest of three to five minutes can recover completely.

[[No single sign decides prognosis after arrest. Weak arms with moving legs may be a watershed injury, man in a barrel, and absent arm movement alone does not always mean a poor outcome.]]

steps.bridge: You've met temperature control four times as a number. Section six is about where that number came from.

lesson.text:
You now hold the targets of twenty twenty-five. The exam's favourite move is to offer you the previous set. So put them side by side.

{{**Target | AHA 2020 | AHA 2025**
Blood pressure | SBP ≥90, MAP ≥65 | **MAP ≥65** only
Temperature | 32–36 °C | **32–37.5 °C**
Duration | ≥24 h | **≥36 h**
SpO₂ | 92–98% | **90–98%**
PaCO₂ | 35–45 | 35–45}}

Take each change with its reason, because the reason is what makes it stay.

Pressure. The separate systolic target was dropped because the trials were all run on mean pressure. Four of them compared a mean of about sixty-five to seventy with a higher one, and found no benefit from the higher.

Temperature range. The top of the range rose from thirty-six to thirty-seven point five, first in a focused update of twenty twenty-three, after the TTM two trial showed that normothermia with fever prevention did as well as thirty-three degrees.

Temperature duration. The minimum rose from twenty-four hours to thirty-six, because the fever that follows early rewarming is linked to worse outcomes.

Oxygen. The floor fell from ninety-two to ninety, on the BOX result. Carbon dioxide didn't change. A trial of deliberately higher carbon dioxide showed no benefit.

[[What changed in twenty twenty-five: temperature control for at least thirty-six hours, not twenty-four; range up to thirty-seven point five, not thirty-six; saturation from ninety, not ninety-two; and mean pressure alone, with no systolic target.]]

The Grand Tests asked this twice. The most appropriate temperature strategy for a comatose patient after an arrest outside hospital: temperature control for at least thirty-six hours. The wrong options were at least twenty-four hours, strict hypothermia of thirty-two to thirty-four for seventy-two hours, and no temperature control unless seizures develop.

The second was an odd-one-out. Which is not a component of post-arrest care: a mean pressure of at least sixty-five, a carbon dioxide of thirty-five to forty-five, a temperature goal of thirty-two to thirty-five, or an EEG if not following commands? The answer is the temperature goal. Thirty-two to thirty-five belongs to no guideline. It was written to sit between the old range and the new one and look familiar.

[[A temperature goal of thirty-two to thirty-five degrees is in no guideline. The ranges that have existed are thirty-two to thirty-four, then thirty-two to thirty-six, and now thirty-two to thirty-seven point five.]]

Then the additions that are entirely new.

Imaging. A CT from head to pelvis, and an echo or bedside ultrasound, may be reasonable after ROSC. The CT finds the cause, such as a subarachnoid haemorrhage, a pulmonary embolus or a dissection, and it finds the injuries of CPR: broken ribs, a torn liver, a pneumothorax.

Glucose. Avoid both ends, below seventy and above a hundred and eighty milligrams per decilitre. There is no tighter target.

Myoclonus without an EEG correlate isn't treated, as you saw. Prognostication now looks for signs of a good outcome as well as a bad one, and a new blood marker has been added. Both wait for the last section.

And recovery. Survivors and their caregivers should have a structured assessment for anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress, with referral, before discharge.

spine: After ROSC, two parallel questions: ST elevation → cath lab; not following commands → temperature control (any rhythm, any location).
Targets (AHA 2025): MAP ≥65; SpO₂ 90–98%; PaCO₂ 35–45; 32–37.5 °C for ≥36 h; glucose 70–180. Old set: SBP ≥90, 92–98%, 32–36 °C, ≥24 h.
Pressure: BOX (MAP 63 vs 77) no difference; 'MAP >80' is a bank key, not a guideline. Fluid only if responsive; noradrenaline first.
STE → emergent angiography, comatose or not. No STE → delayed unless shock, recurrent VT/VF or ongoing ischaemia (COACT, TOMAHAWK).
Seizures ~33%: no prophylaxis; EEG; levetiracetam or valproate; phenytoin fails in myoclonus; no EEG correlate → don't treat.
Early status myoclonus = poor; Lance-Adams = late, action, awake. Electrographic status: ≥10 min continuous or ≥20% of any 60 min.

open.text:
The pulse is back, and it is tempting to feel the work is done. It isn't. Many patients who regain a pulse still die in hospital, and most of those deaths come from the brain.

What follows ROSC is an illness of its own, the post-cardiac arrest syndrome, and it has four parts. A brain injured by the time without flow. A heart that is stunned. A whole-body response to reperfusion, with leaky, dilated vessels, that behaves like sepsis. And whatever caused the arrest, which is usually still there.

So in the first hours two questions run side by side. Is there a coronary artery to open? And is there a brain to protect? Everything in this section serves one or the other.

[[After ROSC, ask two things in parallel: is there ST elevation, which means the catheter laboratory, and does the patient follow commands, which decides temperature control.]]

The trap to listen for is the old number. Almost every target in this section changed in twenty twenty-five, and the banks still carry the earlier values. One key on blood pressure follows no guideline at all.

Begin with the map.

steps.bridge: That is why cold should help. Whether it does help was settled by trials, and they did not agree at first.

lesson.text:
The heart has restarted, but the brain goes on being damaged for hours and days. Temperature control is aimed at that second wave of injury. That is why it is offered only to the patient who doesn't follow commands: he is the one with a brain at risk.

So what is happening in that second wave, and what does cold do to it?

Start with energy. Cooling slows every reaction in the brain. Cerebral metabolism falls by about six per cent or more for every degree. The brain uses less oxygen and burns less ATP, at a time when its blood supply is still unreliable. Marrow asks for the rationale of therapeutic hypothermia after a VF arrest, and its answer is this one: reduced cerebral oxygen consumption.

But that is not the whole story, and the harder question turns on knowing so. Mild cooling protects more than the fall in metabolism can explain. Here is the rest of the chain.

During ischaemia, neurones flood the synapse with excitatory transmitters, above all glutamate. Glutamate opens channels in the next cell, and calcium pours in. That calcium overload switches on the enzymes and the mitochondrial pathways of programmed cell death, apoptosis, which goes on killing neurones for days. Cooling reduces the release of glutamate and of dopamine. Less glutamate means less calcium entry. Less calcium means fewer neurones pushed into apoptosis. Cooling also damps the inflammation and free-radical injury of reperfusion, and it steadies the blood-brain barrier.

[[Cooling protects by several routes at once: lower metabolism and oxygen use, less glutamate and dopamine release, less calcium overload and so less apoptosis. Any option that credits one mechanism alone is wrong.]]

The bank question asked which statement best describes the rationale for the neuroprotective effect, and only half got it. The correct option was the one that listed several pathways together: reperfusion injury, excitatory neurotransmitters, the blood-brain barrier.

The three wrong options each took one true thing and overstated it. 'It primarily reduces metabolism, linearly and uniformly across the brain': metabolism does fall, but neither linearly nor uniformly, and it isn't the main story. That was the most popular wrong choice. 'The primary benefit is cerebral vasoconstriction that lowers intracranial pressure': blood flow falls because metabolism falls, as a consequence, and raised pressure isn't the main problem after an arrest. 'It selectively inhibits apoptosis with little effect on inflammation': the word 'selectively' makes it false.

So when you see 'primarily' or 'selectively' in an option about how cooling works, be suspicious.

steps.bridge: You know the target and where it came from. Now the practical conduct: the probe, the clock, and how it ends.

lesson.text:
Now the trials, in order. There are four moments.

The first is two thousand and two. Two trials were published together, one from Europe and one from Australia, by Bernard. Both took comatose survivors of VF arrest outside hospital and cooled them to thirty-two to thirty-four degrees, for twelve to twenty-four hours. In the European trial a good outcome rose from thirty-nine per cent to fifty-five. In Bernard's it went from twenty-six to forty-nine. Hypothermia looked far better than no treatment, and thirty-two to thirty-four degrees became the standard.

Notice what the control patients got: nothing. Their temperature wasn't managed, and many of them developed fever. Hold that thought.

The second moment is twenty thirteen, the TTM trial. Nine hundred and fifty patients, thirty-three degrees against thirty-six, with temperature controlled in both arms. No difference. So the depth didn't seem to matter, and the guidelines widened to a constant thirty-two to thirty-six.

The third is twenty twenty-one, TTM two. About nineteen hundred patients, thirty-three degrees against normothermia with active prevention of fever. Again no difference in death or function, and more arrhythmias with haemodynamic compromise in the cooled arm.

Now go back to two thousand and two. The early trials didn't compare cold with normal. They compared cold with fever. The benefit may have been the fever that was avoided.

[[Early trials: cooling to thirty-two to thirty-four beat no temperature management. TTM: thirty-six is as good as thirty-three. TTM two: thirty-three is no better than normothermia with fever prevention. What survives is that fever harms.]]

One trial runs the other way, and it explains why cooling is still allowed. HYPERION, in twenty nineteen, studied non-shockable arrests, and thirty-three degrees gave more good outcomes than thirty-seven, about ten per cent against six. It was a small difference in a modest trial. But it is why the range still reaches down to thirty-two, and why non-shockable rhythms are included.

So here is where the guidelines stand.

{{**Era | Target | Duration**
2002–2010 | 32–34 °C | 12–24 h
After TTM (2015, 2020) | constant 32–36 °C | ≥24 h
ERC–ESICM 2025 | prevent fever, ≤37.5 °C | 36–72 h
**AHA 2025** | **32–37.5 °C** | **≥36 h**}}

America calls all of it temperature control. A hypothermic target of thirty-two to thirty-four and a normothermic one of thirty-six to thirty-seven point five both qualify. What isn't allowed is fever. Europe says simply: actively prevent fever, at thirty-seven point five or below, for thirty-six to seventy-two hours, and don't actively rewarm a patient who is mildly cold on his own. The older European wording, fever above thirty-seven point seven for at least seventy-two hours, is from twenty twenty-one.

Now the keyed answers that belong to an era.

The target after a VF arrest outside hospital, keyed thirty-two to thirty-four: the answer of two thousand and two. Pick it when only historical ranges are offered. Marrow keys thirty-four degrees for a comatose survivor of VF. That lies inside today's American range, so it stands. In that same Marrow stem the brainstem reflexes were absent, and the point was that brain death can't be declared this early after an arrest.

And one key that rests on weak ground. Which statement about therapeutic hypothermia is correct? The key is 'delaying initiation increases mortality', and about half chose it. No randomised trial shows that faster cooling helps. The largest test of early cooling gave cold saline before hospital to more than thirteen hundred patients. It found no benefit, with more re-arrest and more pulmonary oedema. So routine prehospital cooling with cold fluid is not recommended. But in that question the other options were plainly false: that it is for all arrests, that it runs forty-eight hours, that shivering is harmless. So the key is the least wrong answer.

[[Routine prehospital cooling with rapid cold intravenous fluid is not recommended: no benefit, more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema. 'Delay increases mortality' is keyed only because the other options are worse.]]

steps.bridge: That is the conduct. The device that does the cooling can be one of five kinds, and the exam asks the sixth.

lesson.text:
Now how it is actually done.

Temperature control has three working parts. A core temperature probe, which is invasive, in the oesophagus or the bladder, because skin temperature is useless and the probe feeds the device's control loop. A safe target. And coordinated, multimodal control of shivering, which the rest of this section covers.

The old teaching gave it a fixed shape: twenty-four hours at target, then twenty-four hours of rewarming. That schedule has gone. The American guideline gives a minimum of thirty-six hours of temperature control in total. The European one gives thirty-six to seventy-two hours of fever prevention.

And it is for comatose survivors only. 'Therapeutic hypothermia is for all cardiac arrests' is a wrong option, because a patient who follows commands doesn't need it.

One principle runs under all of it: it is always better to prevent fever and shivering than to reverse them. Once either has started, you need more drugs and deeper sedation, and those cloud the neurological examination later.

Now the end of it, which is the part that is examined. Rewarming is controlled, and no faster than half a degree an hour. A feedback device usually runs at about a quarter of a degree an hour, which is about sixteen hours for four degrees. Without a device, using ice packs and blankets alone, Marrow's keyed timeframe for going from thirty-three to thirty-seven is about twenty-four hours.

Why so slow? The bank asked for the physiological principle, and only forty-five per cent got it. Rapid rewarming abruptly raises the brain's metabolic demand, at a time when its oxygen delivery is still fragile. Demand outruns supply, and that is a secondary injury.

[[Rewarm no faster than half a degree an hour. Rapid rewarming raises cerebral metabolic demand beyond oxygen delivery, dilates the vessels and drops the pressure, and releases potassium from the cells.]]

The two wrong options in that question are worth taking apart.

The first said that slow rewarming prevents a rapid fall in potassium. The direction is backwards. Cooling drives potassium into the cells, so the cooled patient tends to run low. Rewarming lets it back out. So the danger on rewarming is a rising potassium, and the mistake that causes it is replacing potassium generously during the cold phase.

The second said that rapid rewarming causes a paradoxical fall in core temperature. That is a real thing with a name, afterdrop. But it belongs to accidental hypothermia, where cold blood from the limbs returns to the core as the patient is warmed in the field. It is not the reason for slow rewarming after an arrest.

[[Potassium moves into cells during cooling and out again on rewarming, so rewarming risks hyperkalaemia. Afterdrop belongs to accidental hypothermia, not to rewarming after temperature control.]]

Three more effects of the cold phase are worth a line each. The heart slows, and that bradycardia is expected and usually left alone. The kidneys pass more urine, the cold diuresis, which takes potassium and magnesium with it. And the liver clears drugs more slowly, which matters a great deal on the last card of this section.

steps.bridge: Whatever the device, the body fights it. The patient shivers, and shivering has a ladder of its own.

lesson.text:
Five ways of cooling are on your card, each with one advantage. The exam asks about a sixth.

An endovascular catheter, a cooling balloon lying in a large vein, is the fastest method there is. It also holds the target most tightly and gives a controlled rewarming, because it works on feedback.

Cold intravenous crystalloid is very fast and is available on any ward, and it works alongside the other methods. So it is a bridge until a device is attached. It doesn't replace one, and you've just seen that it isn't used before hospital.

Pads coated in hydrogel, stuck to the skin, are the easiest to use, and they cool and rewarm quickly under servo control. They suit a unit with no endovascular catheters.

Water-circulating pads and wraps are cheaper than the invasive methods, and they allow targeted cooling of the neck.

Ice packs are very inexpensive. That is their only advantage. They have no control at all.

{{**Method | Advantage**
Endovascular | fastest; tight feedback control
Cold IV crystalloid | fast, everywhere; a bridge only
Hydrogel pads | easiest; rapid cooling and rewarming
Water-circulating pads | cheaper; neck cooling possible
Ice packs | very cheap
**Transnasal evaporative** | **brain-selective**; slow, no feedback}}

Now the one the Grand Test asked. Which method is specific to the brain, has few side effects, but is slow to induce and has no feedback control? Transnasal evaporative cooling. A coolant is sprayed into the nasopharynx and evaporates there, just under the skull base, so it cools the brain first. It can be used before hospital, even during CPR. But induction is slow, and with no feedback it can't hold a target temperature. In the PRINCESS trial it didn't improve outcomes.

[[Endovascular cooling is the fastest and cools the whole body. The only brain-selective method is transnasal evaporative cooling, which is slow to induce and has no feedback control.]]

NEET's wrong option is that intravascular cooling is the brain-specific method. Seventy-nine per cent avoided it. An intravascular catheter cools the blood, and the blood cools everything.

steps.bridge: Those were the steps that keep the examination clear. If shivering beats them, the last rung costs you that.

lesson.text:
Lower the core, and the hypothalamus defends it. First it constricts the skin vessels. Then it shivers. Shivering is not a small nuisance. It can double the body's oxygen consumption, it raises carbon dioxide production, and it makes heat, so it fights the device and the brain's metabolic rate rises with it. That is the reverse of what you set out to do. So shivering is suppressed, and 'shivering is harmless' is a wrong option.

How much shivering? The Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale runs from nought to three. Nought is none. One is confined to the neck and chest. Two adds the arms. Three is the trunk and all four limbs.

{{**BSAS | What you see | Marrow's step**
0–1 | none, or neck and chest only | skin counter-warming
2 | arms as well | add sedation and analgesia
3 | trunk and all limbs | neuromuscular blockade under deep sedation}}

The treatment is a ladder, and the order is the whole point. Each rung up adds sedation, hypotension or both. So you begin with what costs nothing.

The first rung is the background most protocols give every patient: regular paracetamol, often buspirone, and warming of the skin. This card is the second rung, for shivering that persists.

Start with the physical trick, because it is the cleverest. The hypothalamus doesn't decide to shiver from the core temperature alone. It takes a weighted mix of core and skin, and the skin contributes about a fifth. So if you warm the skin, especially the hands and feet, with warm air, the body is persuaded that it is warm. The threshold for shivering falls, while the device goes on holding the core where you want it. This is counter-warming. It is not rewarming.

Next, magnesium, aiming for a slightly raised level, about three to four milligrams per decilitre. It relaxes muscle and dilates the skin vessels, and it doesn't sedate.

[[The first answer to shivering under temperature control is skin counter-warming with magnesium, because neither sedates nor lowers the pressure. Sedatives come after them, and paralysis last.]]

That is the bank's key for the initial intervention that spares both the neurological examination and the haemodynamics. It has been asked twice, with only thirty-two and forty-seven per cent right. The wrong options are the stronger measures: opioid boluses, which are a later, sedating step. Cold saline, which makes shivering worse. And paralysis, which is the last resort.

Then the sedatives of this rung. Dexmedetomidine, an alpha two agonist, lowers the shivering threshold with only light sedation, at the price of bradycardia and some hypotension. Propofol sedates more deeply and lowers the pressure more. Either or both may be used.

A second question appeared in two Grand Tests. Moderate shivering persists, and you want the agent with the least hypotension and sedation. The key is dexmedetomidine. Magnesium would be just as defensible, so if both are offered and the stem says nothing has been tried yet, think of the ladder: magnesium and counter-warming first.

Two further agents finish the rung. Ketamine, as a low infusion at nought point two to nought point three milligrams per kilogram per hour. That is an analgesic dose, not an anaesthetic one, and it supports the blood pressure. And ondansetron, four milligrams every eight hours, which has a modest effect.

[[Second-tier shivering control: counter-warming of hands and feet, magnesium to three to four milligrams per decilitre, dexmedetomidine or propofol, low-dose ketamine infusion, and ondansetron.]]

Midazolam isn't on the list. It sedates without doing much for shivering, and it accumulates in the cold.

steps.bridge: The patient is rewarmed and the sedation is switched off. Section seven asks the hardest question: will he wake?

lesson.text:
The top of the ladder is for shivering that continues despite everything on the last card. It has two steps: an opioid, and then paralysis.

The opioid is fentanyl, in boluses as needed. Your card says it is safer than meperidine, which is pethidine, and that needs explaining, because pethidine is the most effective anti-shivering opioid there is. It lowers the shivering threshold about twice as much as it lowers the threshold for vasoconstriction. The trouble is its metabolite, norpethidine. It lowers the seizure threshold, and it accumulates in renal failure. In a brain already prone to seizures after anoxia, that is a poor trade. So fentanyl is used.

Then paralysis, the treatment of last resort. A neuromuscular blocker abolishes shivering completely. So why is it last? Because of what it takes away. A paralysed patient can't show you a seizure, or myoclonus, or a motor response. You lose the neurological examination.

That sets two conditions before the blocker is given. First, the patient must be deeply sedated and given analgesia, because a paralysed patient can't show distress. Your card specifies a propofol or midazolam infusion to a sedation score of minus five on the Richmond scale, and a fentanyl infusion, both running before the cisatracurium. Second, continuous EEG, because seizures are now invisible.

[[Paralysis is the last resort for shivering. Before it: deep sedation to a Richmond score of minus five and a fentanyl infusion. With it: continuous EEG, because seizures can no longer be seen.]]

The bank asked for the next step when shivering persists despite counter-warming and magnesium, and its key was neuromuscular blockade with continuous EEG. Seventy-two per cent. Strictly, the sedatives sit in between. But look at the wrong options: raise the target temperature to thirty-six, or give a large fluid bolus. The principle being tested is that you escalate the ladder, and that paralysis always travels with EEG. Marrow's version uses the scale: shivering of the trunk and all four limbs, a score of three, goes to neuromuscular blockade under deep sedation.

Why cisatracurium? That is the second half of this card, and a Grand Test asked it.

Cooling slows the liver's cytochrome enzymes, by something like seven to twenty-two per cent for every degree below thirty-seven. So any drug that depends on them lingers. Midazolam does, and so does fentanyl. Their effect outlasts the infusion by many hours, and a patient who is still sedated looks like a patient with a bad brain.

Cisatracurium and atracurium don't depend on those enzymes. They break down in the plasma, by Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis. Hydromorphone is cleared by glucuronidation, which is also outside the cytochrome system.

So the question went like this. A patient under therapeutic hypothermia is receiving midazolam, hydromorphone and atracurium. What is the concern? Reduced cytochrome metabolism of midazolam, with prolonged sedation. Seventy-five per cent. The wrong options attach the wrong pathway to the wrong drug: that cooling slows the cytochrome metabolism of atracurium, or that Hofmann elimination clears hydromorphone or midazolam.

[[Cooling slows cytochrome metabolism, so midazolam and fentanyl accumulate and prolong sedation. Atracurium and cisatracurium are cleared by Hofmann elimination, and hydromorphone by glucuronidation.]]

Keep that last point in hand. Lingering sedation is the commonest reason a prognosis is judged too early.

spine: Cooling protects by many routes: ↓ metabolism (~6%/°C), ↓ glutamate and dopamine release, ↓ calcium overload → ↓ apoptosis. 'Primarily' or 'selectively' = wrong option.
2002 (HACA, Bernard): 32–34 °C beat no control. TTM 2013: 36 = 33. TTM2 2021: 33 no better than fever prevention. HYPERION: non-shockable, 33 better than 37.
Now: AHA 32–37.5 °C ≥36 h; ERC–ESICM ≤37.5 °C for 36–72 h. No prehospital cold saline. Comatose survivors only.
Rewarm ≤0.5 °C/h (device ~0.25): fast rewarming → cerebral demand > supply, hypotension, hyperkalaemia. Afterdrop = accidental hypothermia.
Endovascular fastest; transnasal evaporative = brain-selective, slow, no feedback.
Shivering ladder: counter-warming + Mg first → dexmedetomidine/propofol, ketamine → fentanyl (not pethidine) → paralysis + RASS −5 + EEG. CYP slows: midazolam lingers.

open.text:
You have met temperature control four times now, always as a number. This section is where the number comes from.

It is the story of one treatment across twenty years: from deep cooling for a few patients to a wide range for every comatose survivor. The exam asks from every era of that story, and that is exactly why the banks contradict each other. If you know the order of the trials, you can tell which era a question was written in, and answer it in its own terms.

So the section runs in four steps. Why cold might protect a brain. What the trials found, in order. How temperature control is carried out and how it is ended. And then its price, which is shivering, and the ladder you climb to stop it.

[[Every trial of post-arrest temperature agrees on one thing: fever harms the injured brain. The argument was only ever about how far below normal to go.]]

Listen for three traps. An option that credits cooling with a single mechanism. The direction potassium moves on rewarming. And the order of the shivering ladder, where the first step is not a sedative.

Begin with the mechanism.

steps.bridge: Blood tells you that cells have died. Imaging shows you where, and its timing is the tested point.

lesson.text:
When a brain cell dies, its contents leak into the blood. Three proteins are measured, and the exam asks which part of the nervous system each one comes from.

Neurone-specific enolase, NSE, is an enzyme of glycolysis that lives in the cytoplasm of neurones. It marks the neuronal cell body.

S-100B is a calcium-binding protein of astrocytes. It marks glia.

Neurofilament light chain, NfL, is a structural protein of the cytoskeleton in large myelinated axons. It marks axonal injury.

{{**Marker | Source | Note**
NSE | neuronal cell body (also red cells, platelets) | haemolysis raises it falsely; poor if >60 µg/L at 48–72 h
S-100B | astrocytes (glia) | value uncertain
NfL | large myelinated axons | added by AHA 2025; no agreed threshold
GFAP | astrocytes | value uncertain}}

Why measure them at all? Because they are not influenced by sedatives or by neuromuscular blockers. The examination is, and much of the EEG is. You saw at the end of the last section how sedation lingers in a cooled patient. A blood marker is the one test that doesn't care.

NSE is the best studied, and it is the only biomarker in the European algorithm. It is sampled serially, at twenty-four, forty-eight and seventy-two hours, and the threshold is read at forty-eight or seventy-two. A value above sixty micrograms per litre counts towards a poor outcome.

And the trend tells you more than any single value. A level that goes on rising from day one to day two means neurones are still dying. A level that falls suggests a single release, or a false reading.

[[NSE comes from neuronal cell bodies, S-100B from glia, and neurofilament light chain from axons. None is affected by sedation, and a rising series predicts better than one value.]]

That false reading is the first Grand Test question. Which marker of neuronal injury is known for false positives from haemolysis? NSE, at seventy-one per cent. Enolase is also present in red cells and platelets. A haemolysed sample, or a patient haemolysing on an ECMO circuit, gives a falsely high NSE. So you check the free haemoglobin before you trust it. The wrong option is S-100B.

The second Grand Test question took the newest marker out of the ICU altogether. An amateur boxer has a raised neurofilament light chain in his cerebrospinal fluid after repeated bouts. What does it suggest? Axonal injury. Sixty-nine per cent. NfL rises after any damage to axons, including repeated mild head injury. The wrong options were glial scarring and closure of the blood-brain barrier. Glia is S-100B, or GFAP.

[[NSE is falsely raised by haemolysis, because red cells contain enolase. A raised neurofilament light chain means axonal injury, not glial injury.]]

Where does NfL stand after an arrest? The American guideline of twenty twenty-five added it: a high NSE or NfL within seventy-two hours may support a poor outcome when combined with other tests. The European algorithm still uses only NSE, because the NfL assays differ and no threshold is agreed. So 'NfL was added in twenty twenty-five' is true of the American document.

steps.bridge: MRI is the sensitive scan. The scan the patient actually gets first is a CT, and it has one finding.

lesson.text:
Two scans, and they answer at different times.

CT is the early one. It is quick, it is done on the first day, and it shows swelling. But early on it is often normal even in a badly injured brain.

MRI is the more sensitive one, and the sequence that matters is diffusion-weighted imaging. Here is what it detects. When a cell's ion pumps fail, water moves into the cell and is trapped there. That is cytotoxic oedema. Water that is trapped can't diffuse freely, and restricted diffusion shows up bright on the diffusion image. To be sure that the brightness is real restriction, you look at the map of the apparent diffusion coefficient, the ADC, where true restriction is dark. So the measurement is the ADC, and a low ADC is the finding.

Where does it appear? In the parts of the brain that use the most energy, because they fail first: the cortex, the basal ganglia, the thalamus and the hippocampus.

[[MRI is more sensitive than CT after arrest: diffusion-weighted imaging with a low ADC in the cortex and basal ganglia, done at two to seven days.]]

Now the timing, which a Grand Test asked. The window is two to seven days after the arrest. Before day two the diffusion changes may not have fully developed, so the scan underestimates. After about a week the ADC drifts back towards normal even though the tissue is dead. That is called pseudo-normalisation, and the scan underestimates again.

The key to that question was days three to seven, and sixty-nine per cent chose it. The American guideline of twenty twenty-five says two to seven. Older European guidance, from twenty fifteen, said two to five. So choose two to seven if it is offered. If the options are those of the Grand Test, three to seven sits inside the current window and is the key. The wrong options were 'immediately after the arrest' and 'days two to five only'.

For CT, your card adds a rule from the European guideline. If the first CT is normal and the patient is still unconscious, repeat it at seventy-two to ninety-six hours.

The second Grand Test question is harder, at forty-one per cent, and every wrong option teaches a rule of this section. Day six after an arrest, with limited recovery. Which statement is most correct?

'EEG is the most accurate prognostic test.' No single test is the most accurate. That phrase alone makes it wrong.

'No corneal responses at day six means there will be no recovery.' One absent reflex is not enough. The rule needs pupillary and corneal reflexes both absent, and a second, independent sign as well.

'NSE can be used at day six.' The threshold was validated at forty-eight and seventy-two hours. A value on day six is outside the window.

The correct statement was that MRI can assist with prognosis, and that the cortex is the most commonly affected region. Day six is inside the MRI window.

[[A normal early CT in a patient who stays unconscious is repeated at seventy-two to ninety-six hours. NSE thresholds apply at forty-eight to seventy-two hours only, and no single test is 'the most accurate'.]]

steps.bridge: You have the blood, the scans and the EEG signs. Now the route that puts them in order.

lesson.text:
One finding on CT, and one consequence.

Cerebral oedema is seen in about half of patients scanned after a cardiac arrest. The figure varies with how late the scan is done, which is why a normal first scan gets repeated.

The characteristic finding is attenuation of the interface between grey and white matter. Here is why. Grey matter, in the cortex and the basal ganglia, uses more energy than white matter. So it runs out first and swells first. As it takes up water its density falls towards that of the white matter beside it. The boundary you normally see between them fades. Then the sulci and the cisterns are squeezed flat. The measured version of this is the ratio of grey to white density, and a marked reduction counts towards a poor outcome.

[[On CT, global anoxic injury shows as loss of grey-white differentiation with effaced sulci. It is diffuse and symmetrical, and there is nothing to operate on.]]

That last sentence is what Marrow asked. A patient is brought in after hanging, with a Glasgow score of three, and the CT shows diffuse low density with loss of grey-white differentiation. What is the next step? The wrong option is a neurosurgical consultation. There is no haematoma to remove and no focal lesion to decompress. The diagnosis is anoxic brain injury, and the step is multimodal prognostication and an honest conversation with the family.

The discriminator is symmetry. Anoxic injury is diffuse and affects both sides alike. A focal stroke or a haematoma is on one side, and it may have a surgical answer.

steps.bridge: One branch of that route was 'all brainstem reflexes absent'. That branch has rules of its own.

lesson.text:
Now the whole route, for a patient who is unresponsive after ROSC.

The first branch is asked at once. Is a neurological cause of the arrest suspected? A subarachnoid haemorrhage, a stroke or a head injury can stop the heart. If yes, a brain CT comes first, because finding one changes everything that follows.

If no, the patient has temperature control. Then he is rewarmed. If he is still unresponsive, the next step is to exclude confounders, and the one named on your card is residual sedation. You know why from the last section.

Then the brainstem is examined, through four reflexes: pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic and cough. Between them they test the midbrain, the pons and the medulla.

If every one of them is absent, the patient moves to the brain death pathway, which is the next card. If any is present, this is not brain death, and you go on to neuroprognostication.

And here is how the European algorithm does that, because it is the most concrete rule you can carry. At seventy-two hours or later, with confounders excluded, in a patient who is unconscious with a motor response of three or less, which means no better than abnormal flexion, a poor outcome is likely when at least two of these are present.

{{**Poor outcome likely if ≥2 (at ≥72 h, motor score ≤3)**
• No pupillary AND corneal reflexes
• N20 absent on both sides (SSEP)
• Highly malignant EEG after 24 h
• NSE >60 µg/L at 48 and/or 72 h
• Status myoclonus within 72 h
• Diffuse, extensive anoxic injury on CT or MRI}}

[[A poor outcome is likely only with two or more of: absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, absent N20 on both sides, a highly malignant EEG, NSE above sixty, early status myoclonus, or extensive anoxic injury on imaging.]]

Two is the number to remember. One sign, however striking, sends you back to observe and reassess. Of all of them, the N20 absent on both sides is the most specific single test. That is the cortical response to stimulating the median nerve at the wrist.

The last line of the algorithm is about donation. If life-sustaining treatment is going to be withdrawn, or if the circulation fails at any point, the patient is evaluated for organ donation. The guideline of twenty twenty-five makes that a strong recommendation, for every patient who meets brain death criteria and before any planned withdrawal.

Marrow asks how donation after circulatory death is run. The treating team decides on withdrawal and carries it out. Circulatory death follows. There is a mandatory no-touch period of a few minutes, and only then retrieval. Comfort care continues throughout. The donation team is contacted, but it never leads the decision to withdraw. A second Marrow stem had a severe head injury, not brain dead, with a family requesting withdrawal: the answer was to offer donation after circulatory death.

[[Withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment is decided and carried out by the treating team. The donation team never leads it. After circulatory death there is a no-touch period before retrieval.]]

One Marrow key is disputed, so know both sides. A patient after an arrest outside hospital is on propofol and fentanyl, with a Glasgow score of three and pinpoint pupils. The key says neither temperature option is indicated yet. By the guidelines, temperature control goes to every comatose survivor, sedated or not. What sedation delays is the prognosis and the brain death testing. So if you're asked about starting temperature control, start it. If you're asked to judge the brain, wait for the drugs to clear.

steps.bridge: That is the worst outcome. The last card turns the other way: the signs that say he may wake.

lesson.text:
Brain death is a separate question from prognosis. Prognosis asks whether a living brain will recover. Brain death asks whether the whole brain, brainstem included, has permanently stopped. If it has, the person has died.

Three signs make you look for it. Fixed, dilated pupils. Diabetes insipidus. And cardiovascular changes. Each has a mechanism. When the hypothalamus and the posterior pituitary die, antidiuretic hormone is no longer released, so the patient pours out dilute urine and the sodium climbs. When the brainstem loses control of the circulation, there is first a surge of catecholamines, and then the vessels dilate and the pressure falls.

The CT that goes with it shows severe cerebral oedema with brainstem herniation. That scan turns the question from 'how will he do?' to 'has he died?'

Then the determination, which follows the World Brain Death Project of twenty twenty. It needs three things. Coma of a known and irreversible cause. Absence of all brainstem reflexes. And a positive apnoea test, which means no breathing effort when the arterial carbon dioxide has risen to sixty millimetres of mercury or more, with a pH below seven point three. In a patient who chronically retains carbon dioxide, it is a rise of twenty or more above his baseline.

Before any of that, the prerequisites. A core temperature of at least thirty-six degrees. A systolic pressure of at least a hundred, with vasopressors if needed. And no confounding drugs.

{{**Brain death (World Brain Death Project 2020)**
Prerequisites: core ≥36 °C; SBP ≥100 or MAP ≥60 mmHg; no confounding drugs
1 Coma of known, irreversible cause
2 All brainstem reflexes absent
3 Apnoea test: no breaths at PaCO₂ ≥60 mmHg (or ≥20 above baseline), pH <7.30
Ancillary only: EEG, flow studies}}

[[Brain death is a clinical diagnosis: irreversible coma of known cause, absent brainstem reflexes, and a positive apnoea test. EEG and blood-flow studies are ancillary, and spinal reflexes may persist.]]

Notice the temperature. A patient under temperature control at thirty-three degrees can't be tested. That is one more reason nothing is declared early after an arrest.

Two traps. The first is 'an isoelectric EEG is required to declare brain death'. It isn't. The diagnosis is clinical, and the EEG is an ancillary test for when the examination can't be completed. Marrow's key lists an isoelectric EEG together with absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnoea test as criteria that can be used. Read that as what may be used, not what is mandatory.

The second is 'preserved spinal reflexes exclude brain death'. They don't. The spinal cord is intact, so a limb may still move to a stimulus.

And one mimic. In the locked-in syndrome a lesion in the ventral pons cuts every motor pathway. The patient looks unresponsive, but he is fully conscious, and he can still blink and move his eyes vertically. Ask him to look up.
