The criteria are international. The declaration is local. Brain death is confirmed according to the law of the country. In India that is the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, under which a board of doctors certifies it. And once it is confirmed, the patient is evaluated for organ donation.

For twenty years prognostication looked in one direction. Every test was a search for evidence that the patient would do badly. The guideline of twenty twenty-five turns it round, and that is the first of five changes on this card.

One: there are now predictors of a favourable outcome. Three are the ones to know. A continuous EEG background without discharges, within seventy-two hours. A normal NSE. And a motor response of withdrawal or better. The American list also counts an MRI with no restricted diffusion at two to seven days. Each is weak evidence alone, and each is read with the other tests. But they let you argue for continuing, and not only for stopping.

Be careful with one thing that is left off that list. Preserved pupillary or corneal reflexes do not predict a good outcome. Many patients who keep them still do badly. Their absence counts against the patient. Their presence proves little.

Two: neurofilament light chain joins NSE as a blood marker, as you saw. Axons.

Three: the EEG now works in both directions. A continuous background with no epileptiform discharges means a working cortex. Burst suppression, or a suppressed background, off sedation at seventy-two hours or later, means the reverse.

[[New in twenty twenty-five: signs of a good outcome. A continuous EEG background without discharges, a normal NSE, or a withdrawal motor response may support recovery. Preserved pupillary or corneal reflexes do not.]]

Four: myoclonus with no EEG correlate is not treated.

Five is the timing, and it is the one the Grand Test asked. The impressions from all the tests are consolidated at seventy-two hours or more after the return to normothermia, and after sedatives have been stopped. Count from normothermia, not from the arrest.

The stem was a patient on day two of cooling, with absent corneal reflexes and no response to pain. What is the next step in prognostication? Wait at least seventy-two hours. Eighty-three per cent. Cold itself depresses the reflexes, and the sedatives are still circulating. The wrong options were to withdraw now, and to send an NSE to guide an immediate decision.

[[Day two, still cooled, with absent reflexes: wait. Prognosis is consolidated at least seventy-two hours after normothermia and off sedation. Cold and sedatives both make the brain look worse than it is.]]

That is the last card of the packet, and of the cardiology series. So go back to where the series began.

Shock one opened with a single idea. Every shock is one of three numbers failing: the filling, the pump, or the squeeze. For nine packets you have found the failing number and held it up while the cause was fixed. An infarct took the pump. A rhythm took the pump's timing. A drug took the pump or the squeeze. A full pericardium and a clot in the lung took the filling. A torn aorta took all of them in turn.

Cardiac arrest is the three numbers failing together. Nothing fills, nothing pumps, nothing squeezes. Now look at what you did in this packet, in those terms. Your hands became the pump. Adrenaline became the squeeze. Pushing the uterus aside, letting the air out of a tense chest, replacing lost blood: each of those gave the filling back. And the shock cleared the rhythm so the heart's own pump could return.

When it did return, the three numbers came back stunned, and you read them just as you did in the first packet. Only the judge had changed. It was no longer the lactate. It was the brain.

So that is cardiology, from the first failing number to the last question a family asks. Read the three numbers. Find the one that is failing. Support it. Fix the cause.

spine: Markers: NSE = neuronal body (haemolysis falsely raises it; poor if >60 µg/L at 48–72 h), S-100B = glia, NfL = axons (AHA 2025). Unaffected by sedation; trend beats one value.
MRI (DWI, low ADC; cortex and basal ganglia) at 2–7 days. CT: loss of grey-white differentiation, no surgical target; repeat a normal CT at 72–96 h.
Route: neuro cause? → CT. Else temperature control → rewarm → clear sedation → brainstem reflexes. All absent → brain death pathway.
ERC: poor outcome likely with ≥2 of: no pupillary + corneal reflexes, bilateral absent N20, malignant EEG, NSE >60, status myoclonus ≤72 h, diffuse injury on imaging.
Brain death is clinical: irreversible coma + absent brainstem reflexes + apnoea test (PaCO₂ ≥60, pH <7.30); EEG ancillary; spinal reflexes may persist.
2025: favourable predictors (continuous EEG, normal NSE, withdrawal response). Consolidate ≥72 h after normothermia, off sedation.

open.text:
The patient has been kept from fever, rewarmed, and the sedation is off. He hasn't woken. The family asks the one question that matters to them, and this section is how you answer it honestly.

The danger here is not a wrong dose. It is a prophecy that fulfils itself. If you decide too early that the outlook is hopeless, treatment is withdrawn, the patient dies, and the prediction looks correct. Nobody learns that he might have woken on day five.

So every rule in this section is built to prevent a falsely pessimistic call. Wait long enough. Clear the confounders, above all sedation. And never rest the decision on one test.

[[Prognosis after cardiac arrest is multimodal and delayed: no single test decides, and the judgement is made at least seventy-two hours after normothermia, with sedation cleared.]]

The tests come in four families: the examination, the electrical tests, the blood markers and the imaging. The trap to listen for is any option that names a single most accurate test, or that acts on day two.

Begin with the blood, because it is the one family that no drug can confuse.

close.text:
So let's walk back through the arrest, the way it happened.

You started compressions within seconds, because your hands are the only pump he has. You shocked the shockable rhythms early, and kept the pauses short. You gave adrenaline as soon as you could in the non-shockable rhythms, and after the second shock in the shockable ones. You looked for the reversible causes. When the heart came back, you held the pressure, the oxygen and the carbon dioxide in range, and you opened the artery when the ECG asked for it. You controlled his temperature. And you waited, for at least seventy-two hours, before you judged his brain.

Now the traps.

One. Intraosseous access in a patient who is awake. The tempting step is to flush it straight away. [[Flushing an intraosseous line hurts. In a conscious patient, give forty milligrams of preservative-free lidocaine through the line first.]] You missed this one.

Two. Temperature control after the arrest. The tempting answers are thirty-six degrees for twelve hours, or strict cooling to thirty-two. [[Twenty twenty-five: any comatose survivor, any rhythm, held between thirty-two and thirty-seven point five degrees, for at least thirty-six hours.]] Another miss.

Three. Adrenaline in arrest. The tempting answer is one millilitre of one in one thousand. The arrest dose is one milligram as ten millilitres of one in ten thousand. One in one thousand is the strength for an intramuscular dose in anaphylaxis.

Four. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. The tempting answer is a synchronised shock. A polymorphic rhythm can't be synchronised. It's an unsynchronised shock, at full energy.

Five. An end-tidal carbon dioxide of eight during compressions. The tempting answers are bicarbonate or faster ventilation. Low carbon dioxide means low flow. Improve the compressions.

And six. A mother in arrest. The tempting job for the second rescuer is the caesarean or the defibrillator. The second rescuer pushes the uterus to the left, continuously, with her lying flat.

The check comes up on the next screen. Answer each in your head before you tap it open.

And that's the whole of cardiology for NEET. Ten packets, one idea underneath them all. Read the three numbers. Find the one that's failing. Support it, and fix the cause.

drill.q: Conscious patient, IO needle in place. What goes in before the flush?
drill.a: 40 mg (2 mL) of preservative-free 2% lidocaine slowly over 2 min, dwell ~1 min, then flush 5-10 mL (GT8 Q2 miss).

drill.q: 1 mg adrenaline in arrest: what volume of which strength?
drill.a: 10 mL of 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL). 1:1000 is 1 mg/mL, for IM anaphylaxis (34% right).

drill.q: When is adrenaline first given in VF? In asystole?
drill.a: VF/pVT: after the 2nd shock. Asystole/PEA: as soon as access exists. 1 mg every 3-5 min.

drill.q: Refractory VF: the two antiarrhythmics and doses?
drill.a: Amiodarone 300 then 150 mg, OR lidocaine 1-1.5 then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg (ALPS: equal). Child: 5 mg/kg; 1 mg/kg.

drill.q: Which parameter best predicts ROSC during CPR?
drill.a: Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic − right atrial diastolic (needs 15-20 mmHg). Not systolic peak, not a femoral pulse.

drill.q: ETCO2 falls from 18 to 7 during CPR, rhythm unchanged. What do you do?
drill.a: Improve compressions and rotate the compressor: ETCO2 reflects flow. Not bicarbonate, not more breaths.

drill.q: Perishock pause and survival: direct or inverse? Minimum compression fraction?
drill.a: Inverse (36% right). CCF at least 60%; pre-shock pause as short as possible (ERC under 5 s).

drill.q: Definite pulse, only gasping. Management?
drill.a: Rescue breaths, 1 every 6 s; recheck pulse every 2 min. Not 30:2.

drill.q: Choking adult, conscious, 2025 sequence? Third-trimester woman?
drill.a: 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts; in late pregnancy (and infants) 5 back blows then 5 CHEST thrusts. Unresponsive: CPR.

drill.q: Bag-mask CPR: what best protects cerebral perfusion? Main limitation of the bag-mask?
drill.a: Avoid hyperinflation (31% right); 30:2, not 10/min. Limitation: gastric inflation.

drill.q: Polymorphic VT: how is it shocked? Torsades recurring after magnesium in an alert patient?
drill.a: Unsynchronised, maximum energy. More magnesium and stop the QT drugs (60% right); pacing only if that fails.

drill.q: Atropine: indication, dose, maximum?
drill.a: Symptomatic bradycardia only: 1 mg every 3-5 min, max 3 mg (0.5 mg is the old AHA dose; ERC still uses 0.5 mg). First even in complete block, with pacing ready.

drill.q: Adult arrest: first route of access in 2025? Is the ET route still allowed?
drill.a: IV first, IO if IV fails. ET drug route removed in AHA 2025 (old: 2-2.5× dose).

drill.q: Universal termination-of-resuscitation rule?
drill.a: All three: not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC. Never ETCO2 alone; not for trauma.

drill.q: Maternal arrest: most critical modification, and what the second rescuer does?
drill.a: Continuous manual left uterine displacement (from ~20 weeks). IV above the diaphragm; same drugs and energy.

drill.q: Arrest in a woman on a magnesium infusion: next step? Commonest cause of PEA in pregnancy?
drill.a: Stop magnesium, give IV calcium. Hypovolaemia from obstetric haemorrhage.

drill.q: Resuscitative delivery: timing, source of the rule, incision?
drill.a: Prepare at recognition, deliver by 5 min if no ROSC; Katz 1986; vertical midline from just above the symphysis to the umbilicus.

drill.q: Heat stroke: method, rate, when to stop?
drill.a: Ice-water immersion (1-5 °C), at least 0.15 °C/min, stop at about 38.6-39 °C (the '36 °C' key is wrong).

drill.q: VF at core 29 °C: what do you do? Which blood test says stop?
drill.a: Continue CPR and rewarm (ECLS); withhold drugs until above 30 °C (ERC 3 shocks, AHA 2025 one). K above 12 mmol/L = stop.

drill.q: Surugadai ECPR criteria: is core temperature under 35 °C an exclusion?
drill.a: No. Exclusions: non-cardiac cause, ROSC within 10 min, core under 30 °C, pregnancy (42% right). ECPR is always VA.

drill.q: Post-ROSC targets (AHA 2025): MAP, SpO2, PaCO2, temperature and duration?
drill.a: MAP at least 65; SpO2 90-98%; PaCO2 35-45; 32-37.5 °C for at least 36 h if not following commands. Old: 92-98%, 32-36 °C, 24 h.

drill.q: Comatose after VF arrest with ST elevation: when is angiography? Without ST elevation?
drill.a: Emergent, comatose or not. Without STE: delayed, unless shock, recurrent VT/VF or ongoing ischaemia (COACT, TOMAHAWK).

drill.q: Why is rewarming slow, and what happens to potassium?
drill.a: No faster than 0.5 °C/h: rapid rewarming raises cerebral metabolic demand beyond delivery (45% right). Potassium RISES on rewarming.

drill.q: First intervention for shivering under temperature control? Last resort and its conditions?
drill.a: Skin counter-warming + magnesium (32% right). Paralysis, with RASS −5 sedation, fentanyl and continuous EEG.

drill.q: NSE, S-100B, NfL: source of each? Which is faked by haemolysis? MRI window? When is prognosis consolidated?
drill.a: Neuronal body, glia, axon; NSE; MRI at 2-7 days (DocT 3-7); at least 72 h after normothermia, off sedation, never on one test.

traps.trap: Flushing an intraosseous line in a conscious patient without anaesthetising the marrow (or using skin infiltration only)
traps.truth: Infusion pain comes from pressure in the marrow space: give 40 mg (2 mL) of preservative-free 2% lidocaine slowly through the IO needle over 2 min, dwell ~1 min, flush 5-10 mL, then 20 mg more if needed.

traps.trap: 36 °C for 12 h / strict 32-34 °C / PEA excluded from temperature control
traps.truth: Any comatose survivor, any rhythm, any location: 32-37.5 °C for at least 36 h (AHA 2025).

traps.trap: Abdominal thrusts to drain water from a drowned child's lungs; or high-flow oxygen and watch
traps.truth: Drowning is a hypoxic arrest: CPR with rescue breaths first (ERC: 5 initial breaths, then 30:2). Thrusts delay ventilation and cause regurgitation.

traps.trap: Gasping means the patient is breathing, so wait
traps.truth: Agonal gasps are a sign of arrest (up to 40-60% of OHCA): start compressions.

traps.trap: Begin rescue breaths first, or check the rhythm first
traps.truth: Adult BLS is C-A-B: 30 compressions before airway and breaths; the monitor goes on when it arrives.

traps.trap: The perishock pause is directly proportional to survival
traps.truth: It is inversely related (perishock pause 40 s or more vs under 20 s: OR 0.54). The other statements (early VF responds best; repeated shocks lower impedance by 8% or less) are true.

traps.trap: Check breathing and pulse first, then shout for help
traps.truth: Help and the AED are sent for BEFORE the 10-second breathing and pulse check.

traps.trap: Begin 30:2 in a patient with a definite pulse who is only gasping
traps.truth: Respiratory arrest: rescue breaths, 1 every 6 s, pulse check every 2 min.

traps.trap: Check the pulse, or shock again, after one AED shock or after 'no shock advised'
traps.truth: Resume CPR at once for 2 minutes; no pulse check.

traps.trap: Abdominal thrusts first for a choking adult (older AHA answer)
traps.truth: AHA 2025: cycles of 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts, for adults and children.

traps.trap: Unresponsive choking patient: keep giving back blows and thrusts; or do a blind finger sweep
traps.truth: Once unresponsive: CPR starting with compressions; look in the mouth before breaths and remove only a visible object.

traps.trap: Third trimester choking: back blows then abdominal thrusts; or start CPR while she is conscious
traps.truth: Late pregnancy (and infants, and an abdomen that cannot be encircled): 5 back blows then 5 CHEST thrusts.

traps.trap: Two-finger technique for infant chest thrusts or compressions
traps.truth: 2025: heel of one hand (or two-thumb encircling for compressions); two fingers do not reach depth.

traps.trap: The key limitation of bag-mask ventilation is tracheal injury, or that it needs two rescuers
traps.truth: It is gastric inflation (pharyngeal pressure above ~20 cmH2O opens the lower oesophageal sphincter).

traps.trap: In OHCA intubation is always the preferred advanced airway
traps.truth: With low intubation success or little practice, a supraglottic airway is preferred; outcomes are similar.

traps.trap: Advanced airway first, then suction and basic manoeuvres (trauma airway order)
traps.truth: Suction → jaw thrust/chin lift → OPA/NPA → cuffed ETT with in-line stabilisation → surgical airway.

traps.trap: 'Deliver 10 breaths per minute' with a bag-mask to protect cerebral perfusion; or raise tidal volume to 900 mL
traps.truth: With a bag-mask it is 30:2; the answer is to avoid hyperinflation (each breath over 1 s, ~500-600 mL). 10/min only with an advanced airway.

traps.trap: Chest X-ray is the best way to confirm the tube is in the trachea
traps.truth: Waveform capnography confirms tracheal placement; the X-ray shows depth only. (NEET 2025 keyed X-ray where CO2 was already shown and 'proper position' was asked.)

traps.trap: Titrate oxygen to 92-98% during CPR
traps.truth: No saturation target during arrest: maximal FiO2. Titrate after ROSC to 90-98% (2020: 92-98%; ERC 94-98%).

traps.trap: VT cannot support perfusion
traps.truth: VF never perfuses; VT often carries a pulse and is shockable only when pulseless.

traps.trap: AF with a fast rate is a shockable arrest rhythm
traps.truth: Pulseless with an organised rhythm = PEA (CPR, adrenaline). With a pulse it is cardioverted in synchrony.

traps.trap: Wide QRS, no P waves, rate 150 in IHD = atrial flutter or AF
traps.truth: Regular broad-complex tachycardia in IHD is VT until proven otherwise.

traps.trap: Synchronised cardioversion for polymorphic VT
traps.truth: Always an unsynchronised shock at maximum energy; AHA 2025 treats all sustained polymorphic VT as unstable.

traps.trap: Recurrent torsades after magnesium in an alert patient: go straight to pacing or cardioversion
traps.truth: Repeat magnesium and stop the QT drugs (haloperidol, methadone); pacing or isoproterenol only if magnesium fails.

traps.trap: Amiodarone for torsades
traps.truth: It lengthens the QT; it belongs to polymorphic VT with a normal QT (ischaemic).

traps.trap: AF cardioversion starts at 120-200 J, flutter at 50-100 J (older values)
traps.truth: AHA 2025: AF at least 200 J; flutter 200 J.

traps.trap: Halve the energy, or avoid shocks, in pregnancy; or 'only biphasic is acceptable'
traps.truth: Standard energy with no modification; monophasic 360 J is still correct if that is the machine available.

traps.trap: VF after electrical injury: amiodarone, magnesium or pacing first
traps.truth: VF from any cause is defibrillated at once; antiarrhythmics only after shocks fail.

traps.trap: ETCO2 8 mmHg during CPR: give bicarbonate, raise the ventilation rate, or terminate
traps.truth: Low ETCO2 = low flow: improve compressions (depth 5-6 cm, 100-120/min, rotate the compressor).

traps.trap: ROSC requires an ETCO2 of 40 mmHg
traps.truth: 40 was the 2020 algorithm figure. AHA 2025 text: an abrupt, sustained rise (more than 10 mmHg) may indicate ROSC. A gradual climb only means better compressions.

traps.trap: Systolic or peak arterial pressure during compressions best predicts ROSC; or a palpable femoral pulse shows effective CPR
traps.truth: Coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic minus right atrial diastolic) is the best predictor; a femoral pulse may be venous.

traps.trap: Arterial diastolic target during CPR is above 20 mmHg (AHA 2020)
traps.truth: AHA 2025 sets no adult target; ERC 2025 suggests 30 mmHg or more (and ETCO2 25 or more).

traps.trap: 10 mL of 1:1000 (or 1 mL of 1:1000) as the IV arrest dose of adrenaline
traps.truth: 1 mg = 10 mL of 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL). 1:1000 is 1 mg/mL, the IM anaphylaxis strength (0.5 mL).

traps.trap: Phenylephrine, noradrenaline or dopamine as first-line vasopressor in maternal arrest; or half-dose adrenaline
traps.truth: Adrenaline 1 mg every 3-5 min; pregnancy does not change arrest drugs or doses.

traps.trap: Wait for the second rhythm check or an advanced airway before adrenaline in asystole
traps.truth: Non-shockable: as soon as feasible. Shockable: after the second shock (ERC: third).

traps.trap: Vasopressin 40 units is first line or superior after long down-times
traps.truth: No advantage over adrenaline, alone or combined; removed from the algorithm.

traps.trap: Lidocaine + magnesium is wrong for eclamptic maternal VF
traps.truth: Key is amiodarone + magnesium (67%), but lidocaine + magnesium is equally valid by AHA; pick the amiodarone pair if both appear.

traps.trap: No amiodarone available in refractory VF: procainamide
traps.truth: Lidocaine is the alternative; procainamide is for stable VT with a pulse.

traps.trap: Atropine 0.5 mg; or atropine in asystole
traps.truth: 1 mg every 3-5 min, maximum 3 mg, for symptomatic bradycardia only (removed from arrest in 2010). ERC 2025 still uses 0.5 mg (max 3 mg); 0.5 mg is wrong only on an AHA-framed question.

traps.trap: Unstable complete heart block: permanent pacemaker or cardioversion first; post-stenting bradycardia: dopamine first
traps.truth: Atropine first while pacing is prepared; infusions and pacing are second line.

traps.trap: IO first in adult arrest because it is faster; or a subclavian/IJ line after failed peripheral access
traps.truth: Arrest: IV first, IO if it fails (2025). Trauma with 2 failed IVs (or ~90 s): IO next, not a central line.

traps.trap: Adrenaline can be given down the tracheal tube at 2-2.5× the dose
traps.truth: True before 2025 (Marrow key); AHA 2025 removed the ET drug route.

traps.trap: Shock or amiodarone for an organised rhythm at 76/min with no pulse
traps.truth: That is PEA: adrenaline 1 mg and CPR; never shocked.

traps.trap: Paediatric lidocaine 0.1 mg/kg
traps.truth: 1 mg/kg (adrenaline is the 0.01 mg/kg drug).

traps.trap: Lidocaine can be used for AF
traps.truth: Class Ib acts only on ventricular tissue and shortens the QT.

traps.trap: Thrombocytopenia is one of the H's and T's
traps.truth: Thrombosis (coronary, pulmonary) is; thrombocytopenia is not.

traps.trap: Hypocalcaemia or hypomagnesaemia is the electrolyte least likely to cause arrest in pregnancy
traps.truth: Hypernatraemia is: K, Ca and Mg stop the heart, sodium does not.

traps.trap: Chest X-ray to confirm a tension pneumothorax in arrest
traps.truth: Decompress on clinical signs (needle or finger), then chest drain.

traps.trap: An isolated ETCO2 threshold to stop resuscitation; or TOR rules applied to trauma
traps.truth: ETCO2 under 10 after 20 min counts only in an intubated patient as one factor. Universal rule = not EMS-witnessed + no shock + no ROSC; not validated in trauma.

traps.trap: The second rescuer in maternal arrest is for the caesarean or defibrillation; or tilt the patient
traps.truth: The second rescuer gives continuous manual left uterine displacement with the woman flat.

traps.trap: Continue the magnesium infusion in maternal arrest; or hypokalaemia/hypercalcaemia as the cause of bradycardic arrest
traps.truth: On magnesium: stop it and give calcium (hypermagnesaemia). If eclamptic and not yet loaded, the key gives magnesium.
traps.asked: DocT QBank 61%; DocT GT; DocT key 68%

traps.trap: Attach fetal monitors during maternal arrest
traps.truth: Detach them; the fetus is served by restoring the mother's circulation.

traps.trap: Resuscitative delivery after 20 min of failed CPR, only after fetal demise, or after ROSC
traps.truth: Prepare at recognition; deliver by 5 minutes if no ROSC (Katz 1986, the 4-minute rule).

traps.trap: The 'HELP trial' studied maternal arrest and perimortem caesarean
traps.truth: No such trial: evidence is Katz 1986/2005 and Einav 2012 (case series). If the options repeat, eliminate MOMS, ALPS, PROWESS.

traps.trap: Supra-umbilical or xiphoid incision for resuscitative delivery
traps.truth: Vertical midline from just above the symphysis pubis to the umbilicus, at the bedside.

traps.trap: Cool exertional heat stroke to at least 36 °C to prevent rebound
traps.truth: Wrong key: stop active cooling at about 38.6-39 °C (AHA 2025: 38.6 °C). Method: ice-water immersion, not blankets, fans or cold fluid alone.
traps.asked: DocT key, 78% chose it; 59% and 88% on method

traps.trap: Passive rewarming is inadequate for mild hypothermia
traps.truth: Stable mild hypothermia (32-35 °C) needs only passive external rewarming.

traps.trap: Give antiarrhythmics for VF at 29 °C; or 'AHA is more permissive than ERC' in hypothermia
traps.truth: Below 30 °C: continue CPR, rewarm, withhold drugs. ERC up to 3 shocks; AHA 2025 one shock then defer. The permissive AHA position was 2020.

traps.trap: Core temperature under 35 °C excludes ECPR; or ROSC within 10 min is a reason to cannulate
traps.truth: Surugadai exclusions: non-cardiac cause, ROSC within 10 min, core under 30 °C, pregnancy. 30-35 °C is not excluded.

traps.trap: T inversion with chest pain: call the cath lab for immediate PCI
traps.truth: Most immediate step: monitor, oxygen if needed, aspirin. Immediate angiography is for STEMI or very-high-risk NSTE-ACS.

traps.trap: Stable after VF arrest, so no further intervention; or temperature control only after VF
traps.truth: Not following commands is the only trigger: any rhythm, any location.

traps.trap: Target temperature after VF arrest is 32-34 °C
traps.truth: Historical (2002-2010) key; current AHA 32-37.5 °C for at least 36 h. Pick 32-34 only if no current option exists.

traps.trap: Comatose on TTM with MAP 65: increase MAP above 80 mmHg
traps.truth: DocT key, but no guideline supports it: target MAP at least 65; BOX (63 vs 77) showed no benefit.

traps.trap: Wait for a favourable neurological prognosis, or 24-48 h, before angiography in post-ROSC STEMI; or thrombolyse
traps.truth: Persistent ST elevation = emergent angiography with PCI, comatose or not.

traps.trap: No obvious cause after shockable arrest, so emergent angiography
traps.truth: Without STE, immediate angiography has no benefit (COACT, TOMAHAWK) unless shock, recurrent VT/VF or ongoing ischaemia.

traps.trap: EEG activity with post-anoxic myoclonus means a good chance of recovery; LP is essential; phenytoin for myoclonus
traps.truth: Early myoclonic status with a malignant EEG = poor prognosis; EEG not LP; phenytoin is ineffective.

traps.trap: Malignant EEG persisting on propofol and valproate: wait, or stop sedation
traps.truth: Add levetiracetam (though TELSTAR shows suppression does not change outcome).

traps.trap: No upper-limb motor response always means a poor outcome
traps.truth: Weak arms with moving legs may be a watershed (man-in-a-barrel) injury; no single sign decides.

traps.trap: Temperature control for at least 24 hours (2020); or 'temperature goal 32-35 °C' as a component of care
traps.truth: 2025: at least 36 h at 32-37.5 °C. 32-35 °C is in no guideline.

traps.trap: Hypothermia works primarily by reducing metabolism linearly and uniformly; or primarily by vasoconstriction; or selectively inhibits apoptosis
traps.truth: Several pathways at once (metabolism, excitotoxins, calcium, apoptosis, inflammation, blood-brain barrier).

traps.trap: 'Delaying initiation of hypothermia increases mortality' is false
traps.truth: It is the keyed (least wrong) answer, though no RCT supports faster cooling: prehospital cold saline gave no benefit and more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema.

traps.trap: TH is for all cardiac arrests; hypothermia is held for 48 h; shivering is harmless
traps.truth: Comatose survivors only; trials cooled 24-28 h; shivering must be suppressed.

traps.trap: Slow rewarming prevents a rapid fall in potassium; or prevents a paradoxical fall in core temperature
traps.truth: Rewarming RAISES potassium; afterdrop belongs to accidental hypothermia. The reason is cerebral metabolic demand outrunning oxygen delivery. Rate no faster than 0.5 °C/h.

traps.trap: Intravascular cooling is the brain-specific method
traps.truth: Transnasal evaporative cooling is the only brain-selective method (slow induction, no feedback; PRINCESS negative).

traps.trap: First step for shivering: opioid boluses, cold saline, midazolam or paralysis
traps.truth: Skin counter-warming plus magnesium first (no sedation, no hypotension).

traps.trap: Refractory shivering: raise the target to 36 °C or give a fluid bolus
traps.truth: Escalate the ladder; neuromuscular blockade (last resort) with deep sedation and continuous EEG.

traps.trap: Cooling slows CYP450 metabolism of atracurium; or Hofmann elimination clears midazolam or hydromorphone
traps.truth: CYP slowing affects midazolam and fentanyl (prolonged sedation); atracurium/cisatracurium = Hofmann; hydromorphone = glucuronidation.

traps.trap: S-100B is the marker falsely raised by haemolysis
traps.truth: NSE is (red cells and platelets contain enolase).

traps.trap: Raised NfL in a boxer means glial scarring or blood-brain barrier closure
traps.truth: NfL = axonal injury; glia = S-100B, GFAP.

traps.trap: EEG is the most accurate prognostic test; no corneal reflexes at day 6 means no recovery; NSE can be used at day 6
traps.truth: No single test is 'most accurate'; one absent reflex is not enough; NSE thresholds apply at 48-72 h. Correct: MRI can assist, cortex most affected.

traps.trap: MRI brain immediately after arrest, or days 2-5 only
traps.truth: DocT key days 3-7 (69%); AHA 2025 says 2-7 days (older ERC-ESICM 2015 guidance said 2-5).

traps.trap: Neurosurgical consult for diffuse loss of grey-white differentiation after hanging
traps.truth: Global anoxic injury has no surgical target: prognosticate and counsel the family.

traps.trap: The donation team leads the withdrawal discussion; or sedated comatose survivor: 'no temperature control yet'
traps.truth: The treating team decides and performs WLST. Sedation delays prognosis and brain-death testing, not temperature control (Marrow key disputed).

traps.trap: An isoelectric EEG is required to declare brain death; preserved spinal reflexes exclude it
traps.truth: Clinical diagnosis (coma, absent brainstem reflexes, apnoea test); EEG is ancillary; spinal reflexes may persist.

traps.trap: Day 2 of cooling, absent corneal reflexes: withdraw, or send NSE to decide now
traps.truth: Wait: consolidate at least 72 h after normothermia and off sedation.

mimics.tell: Sudden adult collapse (electrical) = call and AED first; drowning, asphyxia, most children (hypoxic) = breaths early.
Gasps are slow, irregular and ineffective, and with no pulse mean arrest.
A definite pulse: 1 breath every 6 s. No definite pulse in 10 s: CPR 30:2.
Pre-shock = last compression to shock; perishock = pre-shock plus post-shock.
Effective cough and speech = encourage coughing; weak cough, no speech, cyanosis = back blows and thrusts.
Chest thrusts for infants, late pregnancy and an abdomen that cannot be encircled; back blows come first in all.
ACLS 'advanced' = SGA or tube; ATLS 'definitive' = cuffed tube below the cords.
30:2 with a bag-mask; 1 breath every 6 s only once an advanced airway is in.

mimics.pair: Capnography vs chest X-ray for the tube
mimics.tell: Waveform capnography = in the trachea; X-ray = depth (2-5 cm above the carina).
Unsynchronised for VF, pulseless VT and polymorphic VT; synchronised for perfusing AF, flutter, SVT, monomorphic VT.
AV dissociation with fusion and capture beats proves VT.
QT on a sinus beat: long = magnesium, no amiodarone; normal = treat ischaemia, amiodarone or lidocaine.
AF irregularly irregular with no P waves; flutter sawtooth, often regular at 150.

mimics.pair: ETCO2 for CPR quality vs for ROSC
mimics.tell: Quality: keep at least 10, ideally 20. ROSC: an abrupt sustained step up, not a slope.

mimics.pair: Coronary perfusion pressure vs systolic pressure in CPR
mimics.tell: The coronaries fill in the release phase: aortic diastolic minus right atrial pressure.
0.1 mg/mL IV for arrest (10 mL) vs 1 mg/mL IM for anaphylaxis (0.5 mL).
After the second shock vs as soon as access exists.
Narrow escape, inferior MI, Mobitz I respond to atropine; wide escape, Mobitz II, anterior MI need pacing.
1-1.5 mg/kg IV/IO for refractory VF vs a flat 40 mg into the marrow before flushing in a conscious patient.
Narrow, fast = mechanical (tension, tamponade, bleeding, PE); broad, slow = metabolic or toxic (K, acidosis, Na-channel blocker).
BLS and universal: 3 criteria. ALS adds not bystander-witnessed and no bystander CPR.

mimics.pair: Manual uterine displacement vs left lateral tilt
mimics.tell: Displacement keeps her flat for effective compressions; tilt weakens them.

mimics.pair: Magnesium before vs during maternal arrest
mimics.tell: Before: the treatment for eclampsia. Arrest on an infusion: the suspect, so stop it and give calcium.
Heat stroke has a normal set-point: physical cooling, antipyretics useless.

mimics.pair: Mild vs moderate vs severe hypothermia
mimics.tell: Shivering present (32-35) = passive; shivering stopped (28-32) = active external; under 28 or unstable = active internal.

mimics.pair: VA vs VV ECMO in arrest
mimics.tell: No cardiac output, so only arterial return perfuses: ECPR is always VA.

mimics.pair: Coronary branch vs temperature branch after ROSC
mimics.tell: STE decides the cath lab; not following commands decides temperature control; they run in parallel.

mimics.pair: Post-arrest MAP vs spinal cord MAP target
mimics.tell: Post-arrest at least 65; 85-90 belongs to acute spinal cord injury.

mimics.pair: Hyperventilation after ROSC vs in herniation
mimics.tell: After arrest the brain is short of flow, so it is harmful; in herniation it is a brief bridge.
Comatose, within 72 h, malignant EEG = poor; awake, later, action-triggered = good survival.

mimics.pair: Seizure vs shivering under temperature control
mimics.tell: Shivering has no EEG change and settles with skin warming.
Temperature control is the umbrella (32-37.5 °C); hypothermia (32-34 °C) is one way of doing it.
Afterdrop (core falling as cold limb blood returns) belongs to accidental hypothermia only.
Counter-warming heats the skin to stop shivering while the device holds the core.
Pethidine is the stronger anti-shivering drug, but norpethidine lowers the seizure threshold.
Neuronal cell body vs glia vs axon.
CT early: swelling, lost grey-white ratio. MRI at 2-7 days: restricted diffusion, more sensitive.

mimics.pair: Global anoxic injury vs focal lesion on CT
mimics.tell: Diffuse and symmetrical with nothing to remove vs one-sided with a possible surgical answer.
Locked-in patients are conscious and keep blinking and vertical eye movement.

mimics.pair: Donation after brain death vs after circulatory death
mimics.tell: Heart beating, dead by neurological criteria vs death after planned withdrawal plus a no-touch period.
Continuous background without discharges vs burst suppression or suppression off sedation.

new_cards.topic: Accidental hypothermia: grades, rewarming and the cold arrest
new_cards.q:
**Accidental hypothermia:**
a The three grades and how each is rewarmed
b The ECG sequence as the heart cools
c Arrest below 30 °C: shocks and drugs (ERC vs AHA 2025)
d The blood test that says stop
e Handling
a: **Mild 32–35 °C** (still shivering): **passive external**: remove wet clothes, insulate, warm room; shivering adds ~1–2 °C/h
**Moderate 28–32 °C** (shivering stopped): **active external** (forced warm air) + IV fluid warmed to **38–42 °C**; room-temperature fluid cools
**Severe <28 °C, unstable or arrested: active internal**: **ECLS first** (1.5–5 °C/h; HOPE or ICE score to select), thoracic or peritoneal lavage if unavailable
ECG: **sinus bradycardia first (SA node)** → AF → **Osborn (J) waves**, long PR/QRS/QT → **VF, most likely <28 °C**

**Arrest <30 °C:** continue CPR and rewarm. **ERC: up to 3 shocks**, then none, and **no adrenaline or antiarrhythmics until >30 °C**; at 30–35 °C double the interval (adrenaline every 6–10 min). **AHA 2025: one shock**, then defer shocks and adrenaline until ≥30 °C
**K⁺ >12 mmol/L** = cell lysis before cooling: non-survivable, stop, no ECLS. Fixed pupils and Osborn waves do not prognosticate
**Handle gently, keep horizontal** (irritable heart); lidocaine does not work in the cold heart; afterdrop = core falls as cold limb blood returns
new_cards.why: ACLS-55 covers only ECLS rewarming and the <28 °C threshold. The bank asked three things no card answers: rewarming by grade (DocT QBank, 47%: passive rewarming for mild hypothermia; 83%: active internal for core 30 °C with Osborn waves), VF at 29 °C (DocT QBank, 53%: continue CPR, withhold antiarrhythmics until >30 °C), and serum potassium >12 mmol/L as the stop signal (Marrow); also Marrow: SA node is depressed first.

card_flags.issue: Card has no line on IO access outside arrest or on IO pain, yet GT8 Q2 (missed) and two DocT GT lines ask it. 'Agonal gasping in up to 40% of witnessed arrests': AHA 2025 quotes up to 40-60% of OHCA. Minor.
Question part b asks the emergency number in India but the answer gives none (the source printed 109). Should read 108 (ambulance) / 112 (unified).
'Definitive airway: ETT / supraglottic airway / i-gel / Combitube' is loose: a definitive airway (ATLS) is a cuffed tube in the trachea; SGA and Combitube are 'advanced' airways, not definitive.
'Abrupt sustained rise (typically ≥40 mmHg) → ROSC' is the 2020 algorithm figure. AHA 2025 no longer prints 40: 'abrupt increase' (2b), supportive text says a sudden rise of >10 mmHg.
Same as ACLS-43: the ≥40 mmHg threshold is the 2020 value; AHA 2025 says an abrupt rise (>10 mmHg).
Part d 'Its drug class' is ambiguous (asked after lidocaine, answered for amiodarone). Suggest stating both: amiodarone class III, lidocaine class Ib.

Per the pack's explanation, a note on the card has the BLS and ALS termination rules reversed: BLS rule = the same 3 criteria as the universal rule; ALS rule adds 'not bystander-witnessed' and 'no bystander CPR'.
Step 3 threshold 'SBP <90 mmHg' is the older algorithm; AHA 2025 frames it as MAP ≥65 mmHg and dropped the SBP target.
'SBP >90' is no longer an AHA target (MAP ≥65 only). 'Noradrenaline first (ERC-ESICM 2025)': ERC-ESICM says fluids, noradrenaline and/or dobutamine without ranking an agent.
'SBP ≥ 90 mmHg' in part a: AHA 2025 gives MAP ≥65 only.
'Myoclonus is more common: 20-25%' reads as if commoner than seizures (33%). It is the commonest TYPE, a subset of the third.
Row 'ERC/ESICM 2021: TTM at 36 °C' is not what the 2021 guideline said (constant 32-36 °C for ≥24 h, avoid fever >37.7 °C for ≥72 h; it did not single out 36 °C).
'Tested at 24 hours and 72 hours': ERC-ESICM 2025 advises 24, 48 and 72 h, with the >60 µg/L threshold read at 48 and/or 72 h.
